idea: Map by state of the share of residential meters that are advanced (AMI) versus old AMR or non-metered, showing which households are still invisible to their utility.
harm_angle: Without an advanced meter a household cannot access time-of-use savings and outages go undetected longer.
caveat: Utility-level rows aggregated to state may double count where territories overlap.

title: Business First Households Last
idea: Slope chart per utility from commercial and industrial AMI penetration to residential AMI penetration, showing operators that wired up their big customers and left households behind.
harm_angle: Households pay for the meter rollout in rates but get the upgrade last.
caveat: Sector meter totals may include zeros meaning 'no such customers' rather than 'none upgraded'.

title: Smart Meters You Cannot See
idea: Ranked bars of utilities by the gap between installed AMI meters and meters actually giving customers daily digital access to their own data.
harm_angle: A customer billed for a smart meter that never shows them their usage cannot fight a wrong bill.
caveat: Digital-access columns may be sparsely reported, exaggerating the gap.

title: Public Versus Investor Owned Rollout
idea: Distribution of AMI penetration by ownership type, showing whether municipal and cooperative utilities lag or lead investor-owned ones.
harm_angle: Rural co-op customers may be structurally last in line for grid modernization.
caveat: Ownership label values unverified; short-form filers may be missing meter detail entirely.

title: Delivery Only Price Per MWh
idea: Dot plot of the seven delivery-only companies showing revenue per MWh delivered by customer class, exposing whether households pay a higher delivery rate than industry.
harm_angle: Households paying a higher per-unit delivery charge than factories are quietly cross-subsidizing them.
caveat: Only 7 rows -- this is a footnote-scale source, so any chart is a callout not a pattern.

title: Delivery Company Customer Mix
idea: Ranked bars of the delivery companies by customer count split by class, a plain descriptive inventory of who these entities actually serve.
harm_angle: Naming who these opaque delivery-only entities serve is the first step to holding them accountable.
caveat: 7 rows total; genuinely thin source, only two honest ideas exist.

title: Paid To Turn Off
idea: Scatter of customer incentives paid against actual peak demand savings delivered, one point per utility and class, showing who spends a lot for very little load reduction.
harm_angle: Ratepayers fund incentive programs that deliver almost no reliability benefit back to them.
caveat: Incentive dollars and savings may be reported on different bases across utilities.

title: Promise Versus Delivery Gap
idea: Slope chart per utility from potential peak demand savings to actual savings achieved, showing systematic overstatement of what demand response can do.
harm_angle: Planners count phantom megawatts as reliability, and the shortfall shows up as a rolling blackout.
caveat: Potential and actual may be defined differently by filer; a systematic gap could be a definitional artifact.

title: Who Bears The Curtailment
idea: Ranked bars by state of the share of demand response enrollment and delivered savings that comes from residential customers versus industrial ones.
harm_angle: If households absorb the curtailment while industry is exempted, comfort and health risk are pushed onto the people with least choice.
caveat: Enrollment counts do not measure how often a customer was actually curtailed.

title: Water Heaters As Grid Batteries
idea: Timeline of grid-connected water heaters enrolled by utility, showing the quiet growth of appliances in homes that the utility can switch off remotely.
harm_angle: A household can lose hot water on a cold morning because of a grid decision it never agreed to.
caveat: Field may be very sparsely reported across filers.

title: Voltage Optimization Coverage
idea: Ranked bars of utilities by the share of distribution circuits with voltage optimization, showing who has invested in the efficiency upgrade and who has not.
harm_angle: Un-optimized circuits waste energy that customers pay for on every bill.
caveat: Only five real columns; zero may mean not reported.

title: Circuit Counts By State
idea: Map by state of total distribution circuits reported, a plain descriptive base layer for how big each state's distribution grid is.
harm_angle: Circuit density is the denominator for every fair outage comparison between utilities.
caveat: Descriptive only; no harm signal on its own.

title: Optimization Adoption Over Time
idea: Timeline of the national share of circuits with voltage optimization by year, showing whether the upgrade is spreading or stalled.
harm_angle: A stalled upgrade curve is money left on the table that customers keep paying.
caveat: Genuinely thin source -- three ideas is the honest ceiling with five columns.

title: Time Of Use Offered To Whom
idea: Heatmap grid of states against customer class colored by share of customers enrolled in any dynamic pricing program, showing who gets access to cheaper off-peak power.
harm_angle: Households locked out of time-of-use rates pay peak prices they had no way to avoid.
caveat: Enrollment counts lack a denominator here -- pairing with a customer-count source is needed for a true rate.

title: Critical Peak Pricing Exposure
idea: Ranked bars of utilities by residential critical peak pricing enrollment, isolating programs where a household can face a punishing price on the hottest day.
harm_angle: Critical peak pricing on a heat wave day is a bill shock aimed at people who cannot turn off the air conditioner.
caveat: Fields may be participant counts or Y/N flags; interpretation unverified.

title: Penalty Versus Reward Programs
idea: Slope chart per utility comparing critical peak pricing enrollment (penalty design) against critical peak rebate enrollment (reward design), showing which operators chose the punitive structure.
harm_angle: The same behavior change is achieved by rewarding or by punishing -- utilities that punish put the cost on the customer.
caveat: Assumes rebate and pricing columns are comparable participant counts.

title: Real Time Pricing Is An Industry Perk
idea: Distribution of real-time pricing enrollment by customer class, showing whether the sophisticated cheapest rate structure is essentially industrial-only.
harm_angle: The cheapest rate design in the country is reserved for the customers who need help least.
caveat: Sparse reporting could make residential look excluded when it is merely unreported.

title: Efficiency Dollars Per MWh Saved
idea: Scatter of incremental customer incentive dollars against incremental energy savings by utility and class, exposing programs that spend heavily for very little saving.
harm_angle: Efficiency program costs land on every bill whether or not the program saved anyone a kilowatt hour.
caveat: Incremental versus life-cycle columns must not be mixed; both exist and mean different things.

title: Who The Retrofits Went To
idea: Ranked bars by state of the share of efficiency incentive dollars going to residential versus commercial and industrial customers.
harm_angle: If households fund efficiency surcharges but industry collects the retrofits, the transfer runs upward.
caveat: Does not capture who paid the surcharge, only who received incentives, so the transfer claim needs a rate source.

title: Overhead Versus Customer Money
idea: Slope chart per utility from customer incentive spend to all-other-costs spend, showing operators whose efficiency budget goes mostly to administration rather than to customers.
harm_angle: Ratepayer efficiency money consumed by overhead never reaches a household's insulation or furnace.
caveat: All-other-costs definition varies by filer and may include measure delivery, not just admin.

title: Short Lived Savings Claims
idea: Distribution of weighted average measure life in years by class and utility, showing where savings are claimed on measures that will not last.
harm_angle: Long-life savings claims justify long-lived surcharges for equipment that dies in five years.
caveat: Measure-life is self-reported and may be sparsely populated.

title: Who Files What
idea: Heatmap grid of utilities against the fifteen schedule flags, showing at a glance which operators file the detailed schedules and which file almost nothing.
harm_angle: Utilities that report nothing cannot be held to account for outages, rates, or emissions by anyone.
caveat: Flag semantics unverified -- a blank may mean 'not required' rather than 'declined to file'.

title: The Short Form Escape Hatch
idea: Timeline of the count and share of utilities filing the short form by ownership type, showing whether reporting burden is drifting downward over the years.
harm_angle: Every utility that slides onto the short form removes its customers from the public record.
caveat: Short-form eligibility is size-based, so growth may just reflect small new filers.

title: Reporting Completeness Ranked
idea: Ranked bars of utilities by how many of the fifteen schedules they filed, with the biggest utilities filing the least called out at the top.
harm_angle: A large utility with thin filings is a transparency blind spot over a large population.
caveat: Fifteen flag columns must be unpivoted; some schedules only apply to certain utility types.

title: The Consolidation Trail
idea: Flow diagram from old utility name to new parent across effective dates, tracing where local utilities disappeared into holding companies.
harm_angle: When the local utility becomes a line item in a distant holding company, the customer loses the nearest place to complain.
caveat: Only 4 rows in this mart -- this reads as a single snapshot year, not the full merger history, so it is a callout not a trend.

title: Merger Events On A Timeline
idea: Timeline dot plot of merger effective dates with the acquiring parent labeled, a plain descriptive record of consolidation moments.
harm_angle: Dating each merger lets a rate change be tested against the moment ownership changed hands.
caveat: 4 rows -- genuinely thin. effective_date may be text and may not parse.

title: Rooftop Solar By Utility
idea: Map by state of residential net-metering installations per thousand customers, showing where rooftop solar is normal and where the utility has effectively blocked it.
harm_angle: In territories with near-zero installations, households are denied the one way to escape a rising bill.
caveat: No customer denominator inside this table; per-capita needs the sales table joined on utility number.

title: What Rooftops Sell Back
idea: Scatter of installed residential net-metering capacity against energy sold back to the grid by utility, showing territories where rooftops exist but export almost nothing.
harm_angle: Low sell-back per installed MW is the fingerprint of a tariff redesign that quietly stopped paying homeowners.
caveat: Sell-back accounting rules changed over time and vary by state, so cross-state comparison is fragile.

title: The Battery Pairing Divide
idea: Ranked bars of utilities by the share of residential net-metering installations paired with a battery, revealing where households can ride out an outage and where they cannot.
harm_angle: A solar home without a battery still goes dark in a blackout, and that split follows income.
caveat: Paired-battery columns are newer and may be null in earlier data years.

title: Virtual Net Metering Is Big Only
idea: Slope chart per state from virtual net metering customers under 1 MW to those at 1 MW and over, showing whether the community-solar mechanism actually reaches small subscribers.
harm_angle: Community solar sold as access for renters is worthless if only large subscribers can actually use it.
caveat: Virtual net metering columns are likely very sparsely reported outside a handful of states.

title: Size Tier Distribution Of Installations
idea: Distribution across the four capacity group tiers of residential installations, showing whether rooftop systems are getting bigger or smaller over time.
harm_angle: Shrinking system sizes signal a tariff that makes it uneconomic to fully cover a household's load.
caveat: Group tier boundaries are not labeled in the columns and need the EIA form definition.

title: Backup Only Generation Map
idea: Map by state of distributed capacity flagged as back-up only versus utility-owned, showing where private backup generation has replaced a reliable grid.
harm_angle: Heavy private backup capacity is a receipt that the public grid failed the people who could afford a generator -- and everyone else just sat in the dark.
caveat: Backup-only capacity is reported only where utilities know about it, so it undercounts unregistered home generators.

title: Distributed Tech Mix By Sector
idea: Heatmap grid of technology slots against customer sector colored by capacity, showing which sectors got solar and which got diesel.
harm_angle: Households stuck with combustion backup breathe the exhaust in their own neighborhood.
caveat: Ten unlabeled technology slots must be decoded against the EIA form; mapping is not in the column names.

title: Utility Owned Behind The Meter
idea: Ranked bars of utilities by the share of distributed capacity they own themselves, showing where the utility captured the distributed market instead of customers.
harm_angle: When the utility owns the distributed assets, the customer pays for them in rates and keeps none of the value.
caveat: Utility-owned column may be null for many filers, which would silently inflate shares.

title: Generators Per Megawatt
idea: Scatter of number of generators against total capacity by utility, separating fleets of many tiny units from a few large ones.
harm_angle: Many small units means many small emission points spread through neighborhoods rather than one regulated stack.
caveat: Generator counts may be estimates for the small end.

title: Losses Customers Pay For
idea: Ranked bars of utilities by total energy losses as a share of total sources, showing whose grid leaks the most power that customers are still billed for.
harm_angle: Line losses are recovered in rates, so a leaky grid is a direct charge on every household on it.
caveat: Loss accounting includes unbilled and theft in some filings, so high loss is not purely physical.

title: Retail Versus Resale Revenue Split
idea: Flow diagram of each utility's revenue sources -- retail sales, resale, transmission, delivery, credits -- showing operators whose money mostly comes from trading rather than serving customers.
harm_angle: A utility earning mostly from wholesale trading has little reason to care about the retail customer paying its fixed costs.
caveat: Revenue components may not sum to the total across all filers.

title: Peak Demand Headroom By Region
idea: Scatter of summer peak demand against net generation plus purchases by NERC region, showing where the margin between demand and supply is thinnest.
harm_angle: A thin margin is the number that becomes a rolling blackout on the hottest afternoon.
caveat: Peak demand and annual energy are different units; a true reserve margin needs capacity data not present here.

title: Power Given Away Free
idea: Timeline of energy furnished without charge and consumed by the respondent without charge, by ownership type, showing who gets free power off the system.
harm_angle: Free power to institutions and to the utility itself is quietly funded by the paying customers.
caveat: These categories are small and inconsistently reported; may be mostly street lighting.

title: Outage Minutes Map
idea: Map by state of average SAIDI minutes without major event days, weighted by customers served, showing where the lights simply stay off longer.
harm_angle: Every SAIDI minute is a real household without heat, refrigeration, or a working medical device.
caveat: Utility SAIDI is not population weighted by default; naive state averages will mislead unless weighted by customer count.

title: The Major Event Day Loophole
idea: Slope chart per utility from SAIDI with major event days to SAIDI without them, ranking operators by how much of their outage time gets excused away.
harm_angle: The excluded storm hours are exactly the ones where people died in their homes, and they vanish from the headline reliability number.
caveat: MED exclusion is a legitimate IEEE standard, so a large gap can be honest -- ranking must control for storm exposure.

title: Frequency Versus Duration Quadrants
idea: Scatter of SAIFI (how often) against CAIDI (how long each time) per utility, splitting operators into frequent-brief, rare-long, and worst-of-both quadrants.
harm_angle: Worst-of-both-quadrant utilities are where a customer both loses power often and waits a long time each time.
caveat: CAIDI is derived from SAIDI over SAIFI, so the axes are not independent.

title: Who Measures Their Own Outages
idea: Ranked bars of states by the share of reporting utilities whose outages are recorded automatically versus manually, showing where reliability numbers are essentially self-estimated.
harm_angle: Hand-counted outage data lets a utility understate how badly it serves its customers with no way to check.
caveat: Flag semantics unverified; the 'other' method columns suggest non-IEEE reporting that is not comparable.

title: Reliability Drift Over Years
idea: Small multiples per state of SAIDI over the data years, showing which states got measurably worse while rates rose.
harm_angle: A state whose outage minutes climbed year over year is one where people paid more for less.
caveat: Year coverage in this mart is unknown; may be a single reporting year, which would kill the trend.

title: What A Kilowatt Hour Costs You
idea: Map by state of average residential revenue per MWh, the plainest possible read of where electricity is expensive.
harm_angle: Electricity price is a direct measure of what a household must give up to stay warm and cool.
caveat: Revenue per MWh is an average, not a tariff; heavy users pull the average down.

title: Households Pay More Than Factories
idea: Dot plot per utility of residential price per MWh against industrial price per MWh, ranking the widest gaps and naming who runs them.
harm_angle: A large household-to-industrial price gap is a transfer from families to large customers, decided in a rate case most people never see.
caveat: Cost-to-serve genuinely differs by class, so the gap needs framing rather than being read as pure subsidy.

title: Bundled Versus Unbundled Prices
idea: Small multiples by state comparing residential price under bundled, energy-only and delivery-only service types, showing whether deregulation actually delivered cheaper power.
harm_angle: Households told that choosing a supplier would save money can be shown whether it did.
caveat: service_type and part columns segment the rows -- summing across them without filtering will double count badly.

title: Price Trajectory By Ownership
idea: Timeline of average residential price by ownership type, showing whether investor-owned utility customers diverged from co-op and municipal customers over the years.
harm_angle: Which kind of utility you happen to live under can decide what you pay for the same electricity.
caveat: Ownership mix changes over time via mergers, so the cohorts are not stable.

title: Consumption Per Household Map
idea: Map by state of residential MWh per residential customer, showing where climate and housing stock force households to buy far more electricity.
harm_angle: High consumption plus high price is where the energy burden crushes low-income households.
caveat: Customer counts are meters, not people, so multi-unit buildings distort the per-household read.

title: Community Solar Facility Prices
idea: Dot plot per community-solar facility of revenue per MWh by customer class, showing whether subscribers actually get a discount.
harm_angle: Community solar marketed as savings for renters is a scam if subscribers pay more per kilowatt hour than the standard rate.
caveat: Facility-level revenue may be allocated rather than metered; the standard-rate comparison needs the main sales table.

title: Where Community Solar Exists
idea: Map by state of community-solar facilities and subscriber counts, showing the handful of states where the model is real and the rest where it is not.
harm_angle: Renters and low-income households outside those states have no path to solar at all.
caveat: 674 rows total, so state cells will be thin and a few states will dominate.

title: Subscriber Mix Skew
idea: Ranked bars of community-solar facilities by the share of customers that are residential versus commercial, exposing projects that are effectively corporate offtake wearing a community label.
harm_angle: A community program dominated by commercial subscribers took a public subsidy meant for households.
caveat: Customer counts may be blank for some facilities.

title: Community Solar Growth Curve
idea: Timeline of facility count and total sales by year, a plain descriptive read of whether the model is scaling.
harm_angle: A flat curve means a promised access route to clean power never opened.
caveat: Year coverage unknown from metadata.

title: The Utility Map Of America
idea: Map at county grain colored by how many utilities claim service there, revealing monopoly counties and the rare contested ones.
harm_angle: In a single-utility county, a household has literally no alternative when service or price is bad.
caveat: County names are text without FIPS, so mapping needs a name crosswalk and will lose ambiguous names.

title: Territory Sprawl Ranked
idea: Ranked bars of utilities by number of counties served, showing which operators span enormous geographies and which are hyper-local.
harm_angle: A utility spread across hundreds of rural counties is the one whose repair crews take longest to arrive.
caveat: County count is not area or customer count; a big sparse territory looks the same as a big dense one.

title: Territory Churn Over Years
idea: Small multiples per state showing counties gained and lost by utilities across data years, tracing quiet territory transfers.
harm_angle: A county handed to a new operator can see service standards change with no public process.
caveat: Requires multiple data years in the mart, which the metadata does not confirm.

title: Short Form Filers Territory Footprint
idea: Map of counties served exclusively by short-form filers, showing the population living under utilities that report almost nothing.
harm_angle: Those counties are national reporting blind spots -- nobody can audit their reliability or prices.
caveat: Requires the short-form flag to be reliably populated at territory grain.

title: The Minimal Filers
idea: Ranked bars of short-form utilities by customers served, showing how many people are served by operators that file almost no public data.
harm_angle: Over a million people can sit behind utilities that never report an outage minute or a rate detail.
caveat: Customer counts here may be estimates by design of the short form.

title: Short Form Price Outliers
idea: Distribution of revenue per MWh among short-form filers with the extreme high end named, surfacing tiny utilities charging far above the norm with almost no oversight.
harm_angle: Customers of a tiny high-priced utility have no regulator watching and no way to leave.
caveat: Small denominators make ratios wildly noisy; needs a minimum customer threshold.

title: Unrecovered Cost Flags
idea: Heatmap grid of short-form filers against the unrecovered flag columns, surfacing operators reporting unrecovered costs that will land in future rates.
harm_angle: Unrecovered costs become tomorrow's rate increase for the same customers.
caveat: Flag column names are unlabeled form-line numbers; meaning must be confirmed against the EIA form before publishing.

title: Vertically Integrated Or Not
idea: Heatmap grid of utilities against activity flags -- generation, transmission, distribution, retail and wholesale marketing -- showing who controls the whole chain.
harm_angle: A utility that owns generation and also sells retail can set the price it charges itself and pass it to customers.
caveat: Activity flags are self-declared Y/N; unverified how many are blank.

title: RTO Membership Map
idea: Map by state of which RTO or ISO each utility participates in, colored by market, showing the seams where market rules change and no market exists at all.
harm_angle: Customers in non-market regions have no independent monitor watching what their utility charges.
caveat: Utilities can belong to multiple RTOs; the seven flag columns need unpivoting and will overlap.

title: Electric Vehicle Fleet Reporting
idea: Ranked bars of states by count of utilities reporting alternative-fuel vehicle activity, a descriptive read of who is participating in transport electrification.
harm_angle: Utilities absent from EV work leave their customers without charging infrastructure they still pay grid costs for.
caveat: Two similarly named columns with unclear distinction.

title: NERC Region Overlap Tangle
idea: Network graph linking utilities to the NERC regions they claim, showing operators straddling multiple reliability regimes.
harm_angle: Utilities spanning regimes can shop between reliability standards, and customers on the weaker side pay for it.
caveat: Region flags plus a single nerc_region text column may contradict each other.

title: The Balancing Authority Directory
idea: Ranked bars of balancing authorities by the number of states they span, a plain descriptive map of who actually keeps each part of the grid in balance.
harm_angle: Naming the operator responsible for each region is the precondition for blaming anyone for a blackout.
caveat: Only 189 rows and 6 columns -- genuinely thin, essentially a reference table.

title: Balancing Authorities Over Time
idea: Timeline of the count of active balancing authorities by year, showing consolidation of grid control into fewer hands.
harm_angle: Fewer grid operators means fewer independent checks when one of them makes a costly call.
caveat: Consolidation could also reflect reporting changes rather than real mergers.

title: Who Balances Your State
idea: Map of states colored by how many distinct balancing authorities operate there, exposing fragmented versus single-operator states.
harm_angle: A state split across many balancing authorities has no single body accountable when the lights go out.
caveat: Reference-grade source; state assignment may be a mailing state rather than an operating footprint.

title: Every Frack Job On The Map
idea: Point map of disclosures by latitude and longitude sized by total base water volume and colored by operator.
harm_angle: Water volume drawn per job in drought counties is water not available to households.
caveat: A projection column exists, so points may be in mixed datums.

title: Water Use Per Well Climbing
idea: Timeline of median total base water volume per disclosure by state and year showing rising water intensity.
harm_angle: Rising per-well water use in arid basins competes directly with drinking and irrigation supply.
caveat: Volume units unverified; outliers may be data-entry errors.

title: Who Drills The Deepest
idea: Scatter of true vertical depth against water volume colored by operator revealing operator-specific drilling profiles.
harm_angle: Deeper, thirstier wells concentrate risk on the communities directly above them.
caveat: Depth may be missing or recorded in mixed units.

title: Fracking On Federal And Tribal Land
idea: Small multiples by state of disclosure counts flagged as federal or tribal wells over time.
harm_angle: Extraction on tribal land raises consent and revenue questions the flag makes countable.
caveat: Flags may be sparsely or inconsistently set by operators.

title: Reporting Version Drift
idea: Timeline of disclosures by disclosure-format version showing when reporting rules changed and what stopped being reported.
harm_angle: Version changes that drop fields are how disclosure regimes quietly go dark.

title: Trade Secret Chemicals By Operator
idea: Ranked bars of operators by the share of their ingredient rows withheld as proprietary based on missing chemical identifiers.
harm_angle: Neighbors cannot test their well water for a chemical whose name the company refuses to disclose.
caveat: Trade secret is inferred from a missing identifier; the source may encode it differently.

title: The Chemicals Actually Pumped
idea: Ranked bars of the most frequently used ingredients by chemical identifier and total mass with known-hazardous substances highlighted.
harm_angle: Naming the top chemicals by mass is the first step to matching them against toxicity records.
caveat: Ingredient names are free text with many spellings for the same chemical.

title: Chemical Cocktail Fingerprints
idea: Heatmap grid of operator against chemical purpose category showing that different operators use materially different recipes.
harm_angle: Different recipes mean different exposures for the households above each operator's wells.
caveat: Purpose is a free-text category needing grouping.

title: Hazardous Chemical Mass By County
idea: County map of total mass of selected hazardous chemicals pumped cumulative over the record.
harm_angle: Cumulative chemical mass in the ground under a county is exposure the residents never consented to.
caveat: Mass column may be sparsely populated; requires an external hazard list to select chemicals.

title: Suppliers Behind The Wells
idea: Network of supplier to operator to ingredient showing which service companies supply the most-withheld chemicals.
harm_angle: Service companies rather than well operators are often the ones claiming the secrecy.
caveat: Supplier and claimant fields may be largely blank.

title: Where Frack Water Comes From
idea: Ranked bars of water source descriptions by share of total volume split by state.
harm_angle: Fresh groundwater used for fracking is drinking water permanently removed from the aquifer.
caveat: Only 23,747 rows against 248k disclosures, so coverage is partial and possibly non-random.

title: Fresh Versus Recycled Over Time
idea: Timeline by county of the share of water sourced as fresh versus recycled or produced water.
harm_angle: Operators that never recycle keep drawing from the same aquifers their neighbors drink from.
caveat: No date column in this model; a time axis requires joining to the disclosure list.

title: Operators Ranked By Freshwater Reliance
idea: Dot plot of operators by average fresh-water percentage across their disclosures and total number of wells.
harm_angle: Ranks the companies drawing hardest on drinking-water sources.
caveat: Description is free text and needs classification into fresh and recycled buckets.

title: Pipeline Incidents on the Map
idea: Point map of significant gas pipeline incidents since 2010, sized by release volume and colored where anyone was hurt or killed.
harm_angle: Every marked dot is a person burned or killed by a pipeline running past their town.
caveat: 2039 rows and gas transmission plus gathering only per the model comment; other pipeline types are not landed, so this is not all pipelines.

title: Operators Who Keep Having Incidents
idea: Ranked bars of operator by incident count over the period, paired with a second bar for total people hurt. Repeat operators separate from one-time bad luck.
harm_angle: An operator with fifteen significant incidents and no visible consequence is a regulatory failure with casualties.
caveat: No penalty or enforcement column here, so the absence of consequence must be joined from elsewhere, not asserted.

title: Who Dies in Pipeline Accidents
idea: Stacked bars over years of fatalities and injuries broken into public, employee, contractor, and emergency responder. Shows whether the burden falls on workers or bystanders.
harm_angle: Contractors and first responders often absorb the deaths that operators report as routine workplace incidents.
caveat: Small counts per year; a single bad event will dominate a whole year's bar.

title: Release Volume Versus Shutdown Response
idea: Scatter of release volume against whether the operator shut down due to the accident, colored by commodity. Big releases with no shutdown are the ones to ask about.
harm_angle: Continuing to run a line after a large release puts the next town at risk.
caveat: Shutdown indicator semantics unclear; volume units may vary by commodity and need normalizing.

title: Reporting Lag by Operator
idea: Distribution of days from the incident's local time to the report received date, per operator. Slow reporters are a pattern, not an accident.
harm_angle: Late reporting delays every downstream warning to the people living on the line.
caveat: Timezone handling across local_datetime and time_zone could produce false lag.

title: Map of abandoned wells
idea: Point map of all orphaned oil and gas wells, coloured by status and type. The clusters are the places nobody is coming back to plug.
harm_angle: Orphaned wells leak methane and brine into the groundwater of whoever still lives there, with no owner left to bill.
caveat: Lat/long parsed with try_to_number over text; some records rely on township-range descriptions instead and will have no point.

title: Orphan burden by county
idea: Choropleth of orphaned wells per county, the plain map of which local governments inherited the cleanup bill.
harm_angle: Rural counties with no tax base are left holding thousands of wells that the operators walked away from.
caveat: County text is not FIPS-coded; joining to boundaries needs a name match that will fail on duplicates across states.

title: Which states admit their orphans
idea: Ranked bars of orphan counts by state alongside the reporting source for each state, showing that the count reflects state willingness to report as much as reality.
harm_angle: States that under-report orphaned wells leave residents living next to hazards that officially do not exist.
caveat: SOURCE field meaning unverified; differing state definitions of orphaned make cross-state counts genuinely non-comparable.

title: Status mix by state
idea: Heatmap grid of state against well status category, showing where wells are merely idle versus formally orphaned versus plugged.
harm_angle: The gap between idle and orphaned is where operators park liabilities they intend never to pay.
caveat: STATUS vocabulary differs by reporting state and needs harmonising before the grid means anything.

title: Named-operator ghosts in the notes
idea: Text-mined ranked bars of company names appearing in the well-info and other notes fields, reconstructing who abandoned wells the structured fields no longer credit.
harm_angle: Orphaned means the operator is gone on paper; the notes are often the only surviving record of who left the mess.
caveat: Notes fields may be mostly null or purely locational; company-name extraction from free text is error-prone.

source_names: Ember Yearly and Monthly Electricity Data
title: Coal's last holdouts
idea: Share of generation from coal by country and year, small multiples ordered by how late each country peaks. Shows who is still building the dirtiest grid while the rest transition.
harm_angle: People living downwind of coal plants in the countries that never transitioned bear the health cost of the global lag.
caveat: Category/subcategory/variable taxonomy unverified; share vs absolute may require deriving a denominator per country-year.

source_names: Ember Yearly and Monthly Electricity Data
title: Per-capita emissions vs grid mix
idea: Scatter of emissions-intensity metric against fossil share per country-year, animated by year, with OECD/G20 flags used for coloring.
harm_angle: Rich-country grids get cleaner while poorer geographies carry rising intensity, exposing who is left with the dirty power.
caveat: Emissions intensity may not be a stored variable; may need derivation from value rows.

source_names: Ember Yearly and Monthly Electricity Data
title: Demand growth outrunning clean build
idea: Slope chart per country from earliest to latest year comparing demand growth against clean generation growth; countries where demand outruns clean build are the ones adding fossil capacity.
harm_angle: Populations in countries where demand outpaces clean build get locked into decades more fossil combustion.
caveat: yoy_pct_change population unknown; variable names for demand vs clean generation unverified.

source_names: Ember Yearly and Monthly Electricity Data
title: The G7 vs everyone else gap
idea: Ranked bars of latest-year fossil share, with G7/G20/EU/ASEAN/OECD membership flags as row shading, to show whether the rich-country bloc actually leads or trails.
harm_angle: Frames whether the countries that set global climate policy are actually the cleanest, or just the loudest.
caveat: area_type may mix aggregates with countries; aggregate rows must be filtered out or the ranking is meaningless.

source_names: Ember Yearly and Monthly Electricity Data
title: Import dependence heatmap
idea: Heatmap grid of country by year colored by electricity imports as share of demand, revealing which populations depend on a neighbor's grid.
harm_angle: Import-dependent populations are exposed to blackouts and price shocks driven by another government's decisions.
caveat: Import variable presence unverified; many countries may have sparse import rows.

source_names: OWID Fossil fuel share of primary energy
title: Fossil share decline race
idea: Timeline of fossil share by country with a small-multiple grid, ordered by how fast the share fell over the last decade.
harm_angle: Shows which populations are still breathing combustion products because their grid never moved.
caveat: Coverage varies by country; sparse early years may make slopes noisy.

source_names: OWID Fossil fuel share of primary energy
title: Countries going backwards
idea: Ranked bars of countries whose fossil share rose over the last decade, the reversal list nobody publishes.
harm_angle: Reversal countries are re-locking their populations into fossil dependence.
caveat: Requires both endpoint years present per country; missing endpoints silently drop countries.

source_names: OWID Fossil fuel share of primary energy
title: Fossil share vs national wealth
idea: Scatter of fossil share against year, colored by region, to test whether transition is a rich-country privilege.
harm_angle: If only wealthy countries can decarbonize, the transition burden lands on people who cannot afford it.
caveat: No wealth or region column in this table -- region must come from a sibling OWID table.

title: Hazardous Air Pollutant Hot Spots
idea: Ranked bars of facilities by total annual emissions of pollutants flagged as hazardous air pollutants or VOCs, naming the biggest single-site sources in the country.
harm_angle: HAP emissions map directly onto cancer and asthma rates in the fenceline neighborhoods around each site.
caveat: Units vary by pollutant row; summing across unit_of_measure without normalizing is a fatal error.

title: Emissions Trend Per Facility
idea: Small multiples of annual emissions by reporting year for the top emitting facilities, showing which sites cleaned up and which quietly grew.
harm_angle: A facility whose emissions rose year over year did so onto the same people, with nothing stopping it.
caveat: Reporting-year coverage and whether NEI years are triennial is unverified; gaps may look like drops.

title: Which Program Reports Which Pollutant
idea: Heatmap grid of reporting program acronym against pollutant class, showing which pollutants are only ever visible through one program and would vanish if it stopped.
harm_angle: A pollutant tracked by only one program is one budget cut away from being invisible to the public.
caveat: Program acronym coverage may be uneven across years.

title: The Pollutant Long Tail
idea: Distribution of how many distinct facilities report each pollutant, surfacing rare and exotic chemicals reported by only a handful of sites.
harm_angle: A chemical emitted by three plants in the country means three communities carrying an exposure nobody studies.
caveat: Pollutant names may have spelling variants that split the same chemical into several rows.

title: Estimated Versus Measured Emissions
idea: Ranked bars of facilities by the share of their reported emissions carrying an estimation NEI type rather than a measured one, showing whose numbers are essentially guesses.
harm_angle: Enforcement and health studies rest on numbers the polluter estimated for itself.
caveat: nei_type values are undocumented in the model; the measured-versus-estimated split must be confirmed.

title: Air Monitors And The Gaps
idea: Map of every air quality monitoring site as a point, with counties containing no active monitor shaded, showing where nobody is measuring the air at all.
harm_angle: A county with no monitor cannot prove its air is bad, so it never qualifies for relief.
caveat: Coverage gaps need a county universe joined in; closed-date nulls must be treated as still open.

title: Monitors Turned Off
idea: Timeline of monitor establishment versus closure dates by state, showing periods when states retired more air monitors than they opened.
harm_angle: Closing monitors makes bad air legally invisible without improving it by a single molecule.
caveat: Date columns may be text and may not parse cleanly; closure may also reflect a relocation.

title: Monitors Placed Where It Looks Good
idea: Ranked bars by state of the share of monitors sited in rural or residential land-use settings versus industrial ones, questioning whether the network samples where the pollution actually is.
harm_angle: Monitors placed away from industry produce clean readings for a community that is not breathing clean air.
caveat: Land use and setting are self-described categories; siting rules legitimately require some background sites.

title: Tribal Land Monitoring Coverage
idea: Map of monitors on or near tribal lands with the tribe named, showing which nations have air monitoring and which have none.
harm_angle: Tribal nations without monitors cannot document exposure from nearby industry on their own land.
caveat: tribe_name is likely mostly blank; a blank does not mean the site is off tribal land.

title: Who Owns The Monitors
idea: Ranked bars of owning agencies by monitor count and by how many they have closed, showing whether state, local, tribal or federal bodies run the network.
harm_angle: When a polluting state runs its own monitors, the referee works for one team.
caveat: Agency strings are unnormalized free text.

title: The penalty gap map
idea: County map colored by the count of facilities with four or more quarters of noncompliance but under a thousand dollars in penalties - the model already computes this flag.
harm_angle: Communities live next to chronically noncompliant facilities that never get fined.
caveat: 3.1M facility rows include many trivial and inactive registrations; filter to active and major facilities or the map is noise.

title: Inspection drought by neighborhood demographics
idea: Scatter of days since last inspection against percent minority population around the facility, one dot per facility, with a trend line.
harm_angle: If inspectors visit facilities in minority neighborhoods less often, enforcement itself is unequal.
caveat: Percent minority is the agency's own area estimate around the facility; correlation is not causation and industry mix confounds it.

title: Penalty per quarter of noncompliance by state
idea: Ranked bars of median penalty dollars per noncompliant quarter by state, showing which states functionally do not fine polluters.
harm_angle: Weak-penalty states leave residents breathing and drinking the consequences.
caveat: State delegation of federal programs varies so raw penalty comparisons need program-level control.

title: Toxic releases on tribal land
idea: Map of facilities flagged as being in Indian country sized by total toxic releases and transfers, colored by compliance status.
harm_angle: Tribal communities face releases under a jurisdictional regime with thinner enforcement.
caveat: The tribal-land flag is a coarse determination and may miss facilities just outside boundaries.

title: Significant noncompliance without formal action
idea: Heatmap grid of state against EPA region showing the share of significant-noncompliance facilities with zero formal actions - the do-nothing regions.
harm_angle: A facility flagged as seriously noncompliant with no action taken is a regulator that stopped regulating.
caveat: Formal action counts are lifetime totals with no date bound in this column set.

title: Population density around the worst polluters
idea: Scatter of surrounding population density against toxic on-site releases, so the top-right corner names facilities releasing most where most people live.
harm_angle: Highest release plus highest density is the largest number of people exposed.
caveat: Release volume is not toxicity-weighted so a large volume of a mild chemical outranks a small volume of a severe one.

title: Dirtiest Power Per Megawatt Hour
idea: Scatter of plant annual net generation against CO2 equivalent output emission rate, sized by capacity and colored by primary fuel, isolating plants producing little power for enormous pollution.
harm_angle: A high-rate low-output plant dumps pollution on its neighbors for almost no public benefit.
caveat: Single year 2022 snapshot -- no trend possible from this table alone.

title: Peaker Plants In Neighborhoods
idea: Map of plants with low capacity factor but high NOx output rate, points sized by ozone-season NOx tons, showing the peakers that fire on the worst air days.
harm_angle: Peakers run precisely on hot smog days, adding NOx exactly when asthma cases spike.
caveat: Lat/lon are cast with try_to_double so bad rows silently become null and drop off the map.

title: Mercury Rate Outliers
idea: Ranked bars of plants by annual mercury emission rate per MWh, colored by whether the plant burns coal, naming the worst mercury sources in the country.
harm_angle: Mercury accumulates in local fish and in the children who eat them.
caveat: Mercury columns come as raw text in this model and only some rate columns are cast to double.

title: Adjusted Versus Unadjusted Emissions
idea: Slope chart per plant from unadjusted annual emissions to reported adjusted emissions for CO2 and NOx, showing how much pollution the biomass and CHP adjustments remove on paper.
harm_angle: An accounting adjustment that erases tons on paper changes nothing about what the neighborhood inhales.
caveat: The adjustments are methodologically defensible; framing them as hiding pollution without that context would be unfair.

title: Grid Region Carbon Intensity
idea: Heatmap grid of eGRID subregions against fuel category colored by average CO2 rate, showing which regional grids are structurally dirty regardless of individual plants.
harm_angle: Everyone plugged into a dirty subregion carries its emissions no matter what appliance they buy.
caveat: Regional averages must be generation-weighted; a simple mean over plants is misleading.

title: What a five-thousand-row API slice actually contains
idea: Distribution of the populated versus blank rate for each column in the sample, making plain that the id columns are empty and this is shape-testing data only.
key_fields: all columns in the facility sample
harm_angle: Treating a sample as the full dataset produces confidently wrong conclusions about who is polluting.
caveat: The model comment says explicitly this is a 5,000-row slice of one program table with blank facility ids - it is not analysable as environmental data.

title: Facility name duplication in the slice
idea: Ranked bars of the most repeated facility-name strings in the sample, a quick look at how messy name-only matching would be against other sources.
key_fields: facility name column in the sample
harm_angle: Name-only matching produces false links that wrongly accuse or wrongly clear a company.
caveat: Sample-only and no keys; genuinely thin - two ideas is the honest ceiling for this source.

title: Every Regulated Facility Mapped
idea: Dot-density map of all 3.3 million regulated facilities, showing the true industrial footprint of the country at point grain.
harm_angle: Seeing the full density is how a neighborhood discovers it is surrounded by dozens of regulated sites.
caveat: Lat/lon population rate is unknown; a large share of FRS records historically lack coordinates.

title: Facility Burden Per County
idea: Map at county grain of regulated facilities per square mile, ranking the counties carrying the densest industrial load.
harm_angle: The densest counties are where cumulative exposure stacks and no single permit accounts for the total.
caveat: County names are text without FIPS and duplicate across states; needs careful keying.

title: EPA Regions Unequal Load
idea: Ranked bars of the ten EPA regions by facility count and by facilities per staff-equivalent proxy, showing which regional office oversees an impossible caseload.
harm_angle: An overloaded regional office means inspections that never happen in somebody's neighborhood.
caveat: No staffing data in this table -- the workload read requires an outside denominator.

title: One Address Many Facilities
idea: Ranked bars of street addresses hosting many distinct registry ids, exposing industrial complexes that are permitted as separate facilities.
harm_angle: Splitting one complex into many permits keeps each one under the threshold that would trigger real scrutiny.
caveat: Address strings are unnormalized; genuine industrial parks will dominate the top of the list.

title: Industry Mix Of The Regulated Universe
idea: Ranked bars of NAICS codes by number of distinct regulated facilities, a plain descriptive read of which industries dominate the environmental register.
harm_angle: Naming the dominant industries is the first step to asking who oversees them.
caveat: A facility carries multiple NAICS rows, so counting rows instead of distinct registry ids will overstate.

title: Facilities Wearing Many Industry Hats
idea: Distribution of how many distinct NAICS codes each facility claims, surfacing sites with sprawling self-declared industry classifications.
harm_angle: A facility that classifies itself many ways can pick the least-regulated identity when it matters.
caveat: Multiple NAICS is often legitimate multi-process operation, not gaming.

title: Which Programs Classify Which Industries
idea: Heatmap grid of reporting program against NAICS sector, showing which industries are only ever seen through a single regulatory program.
harm_angle: An industry visible to only one program has only one chance of being caught.
caveat: Four-column bridge table -- genuinely thin, no dates and no geography of its own.

title: How Many Programs Watch Each Site
idea: Distribution of how many distinct regulatory programs link to each facility, with the most and least watched sites called out.
harm_angle: A large facility under only one program is a site nobody is fully looking at.
caveat: Program links reflect what a facility triggered, so few links can simply mean a small operation.

title: Program Coverage Map
idea: Map at state grain colored by average number of program links per facility, showing states where the same kind of facility carries far fewer oversight hooks.
harm_angle: Living in a low-linkage state means the plant next door answers to fewer rules than the identical plant elsewhere.
caveat: Program participation is partly delegated to states with different systems, so linkage counts are not purely comparable.

title: The Same Plant Many Names
idea: Network graph of registry ids to the many primary names recorded across programs, exposing facilities that appear under different identities in different systems.
harm_angle: Name drift across systems is how a repeat violator escapes being recognized as a repeat violator.
caveat: Name variation is often benign spelling difference; needs a similarity threshold to be meaningful.

title: Foreign And Territory Facilities
idea: Ranked bars of country and territory codes by facility count, surfacing the regulated sites outside the fifty states that reporting usually forgets.
harm_angle: Territories like Puerto Rico and Guam host regulated industry with far less public attention on it.
caveat: Country field may be almost entirely one value, leaving a tiny tail.

title: The Legacy Industry Register
idea: Ranked bars of SIC codes by distinct facilities, showing which industries are still tracked under the retired classification system.
harm_angle: Facilities still coded only under a retired system are harder to find in any modern analysis.
caveat: Four-column bridge; SIC is deprecated so coverage skews to older records.

title: Facilities With SIC But No NAICS
idea: Ranked bars of programs by count of facilities carrying an SIC code but no modern NAICS classification, exposing records stranded in the old system.
harm_angle: A facility invisible to modern industry-based analysis is one that never shows up in any sector-wide accountability sweep.
caveat: Requires the NAICS bridge table to establish absence, so strictly this is cross-table within the same FRS family.

title: SIC Sprawl Per Facility
idea: Distribution of distinct SIC codes per facility, showing sites with many legacy classifications stacked up over decades.
harm_angle: Accumulated stale classifications make a facility's real business unreadable to the public.
caveat: Genuinely thin source -- three columns of substance, no dates or geography.

title: Regulated Facility Density by Block
idea: Map every registered facility as a point, then shade census blocks by how many regulated facilities sit inside. Viewer sees the pockets of the country that carry a stacked industrial load.
harm_angle: Residents of a handful of blocks live inside a cluster of dozens of regulated facilities while most blocks have none.
caveat: Lat/lon quality varies; accuracy_value and collect_desc suggest some points are ZIP-centroid guesses, which would fake clusters.

title: Which Programs a Facility Is Under
idea: Rank the combinations of EPA program acronyms attached to facilities to show which sites are tracked by many programs versus one. A facility under six programs is a different animal than one under a single program.
harm_angle: Multi-program sites concentrate risk on their neighbors but are regulated piecemeal by separate offices.
caveat: pgm_sys_acrnms is a delimited string; parsing rules unknown from metadata.

title: Facilities Never Updated Since Registration
idea: Plot create_date against update_date per facility; points on the diagonal are records the agency has not touched since the day they were created. Reveals the stale half of the national registry.
harm_angle: Stale registry entries mean nobody has verified whether a facility near you still operates or under what permit.
caveat: Both dates are try_to_date over text; nulls may dominate and would need to be shown, not dropped.

title: Federal Facilities on Tribal Land
idea: Small multiples by federal agency, each showing facilities flagged as sitting on tribal land. Surfaces which arms of the government put regulated operations on tribal ground.
harm_angle: Tribal communities absorb federal industrial siting decisions they had little say in.
caveat: tribal_land_code fill rate unknown; may be sparse enough to be anecdote rather than pattern.

title: The Border Industrial Corridor
idea: Filter to the US-Mexico border indicator and map facility type along the corridor. Shows what kind of industry clusters on the border strip specifically.
harm_angle: Border communities host industry sited to be near a line rather than near oversight.
caveat: Border indicator may be a rarely-populated legacy flag.

title: Greenhouse Emitters Ranked
idea: Ranked bars of facilities by total CO2 equivalent emissions for the latest reporting year, naming the largest reported climate polluters.
harm_angle: The largest emitters set the climate damage that lands hardest on the poorest communities.
caveat: gas_id and sector_id are numeric codes with no label table visible; naming sectors needs a lookup.

title: Which Gas Where
idea: Heatmap grid of sector against gas colored by CO2 equivalent tonnage, showing which industries dominate methane versus CO2 versus fluorinated gases.
harm_angle: Methane-heavy sectors cause near-term warming and local health harm that CO2 totals hide.
caveat: Sector and gas codes unlabeled; totals may double count if subsector rows nest inside sector rows.

title: Facilities That Grew While Everyone Shrank
idea: Slope chart per facility from earliest to latest reporting year of CO2 equivalent emissions, filtered to those that rose against a falling sector trend.
harm_angle: A facility expanding its emissions while its peers cut is a specific, nameable actor doing specific harm.
caveat: Facilities entering and leaving the program between years will produce false rises and falls.

title: The Emission Distribution Tail
idea: Distribution of facility-level CO2 equivalent emissions on a log scale by sector, showing how concentrated total emissions are in a handful of sites.
harm_angle: If a tiny number of sites cause most emissions, action against a short list would help everyone.
caveat: co2e_emission may be null for some gases where only raw emission is reported.

title: Parent Company Emissions Map
idea: Map of reporting facilities as points colored by parent company, letting the viewer see one corporation's national pollution footprint at once.
harm_angle: Seeing a parent's whole footprint moves accountability from the local plant manager to the corporation that owns it.
caveat: parent_company is free text and may hold multiple names in one field; needs normalization before grouping.

title: Who Stopped Reporting
idea: Timeline of facilities by reporting status across years, surfacing sites that dropped out of the greenhouse gas program without closing.
harm_angle: A facility that exits the reporting program keeps emitting but stops being counted.
caveat: Exit can be a legitimate drop below the reporting threshold; needs the emission table to distinguish.

title: Tribal Land Emitters
idea: Map of reporting facilities on tribal land, named with parent company, showing which corporations emit on tribal territory.
harm_angle: Tribal nations often host emissions from operations they did not permit and do not profit from.
caveat: tribal_land_id is likely mostly null; nulls must not be read as 'not on tribal land'.

title: Self Monitoring Versus Instruments
idea: Ranked bars of sectors by the share of facilities using continuous emissions monitoring versus calculation-based methods, showing where reported numbers are computed rather than measured.
harm_angle: Sectors that calculate rather than measure their own emissions are the ones whose numbers can be quietly wrong.
caveat: cems_used may be a Y/N flag with heavy blanks; blank does not mean 'no monitor'.

title: Carbon Capture Claims Versus Scale
idea: Scatter of CO2 captured against emitted CO2 supplied per facility, showing how small capture actually is relative to what the same facilities emit.
harm_angle: Communities are asked to accept a plant staying open because of a capture claim that may be a rounding error.
caveat: Capture columns are likely populated for only a tiny handful of facilities.

title: High Priority Violators Map
idea: Map of air facilities currently flagged as high priority violators, colored by operating status, showing where the worst air offenders are still running.
harm_angle: An HPV flag means documented serious violation -- and the people next door are still breathing it today.
caveat: current_hpv is a point-in-time flag with no date, so we cannot see how long a site has held it.

title: Major Sources In Dense Zips
idea: Map at ZIP grain of the count of facilities classed as major air pollutant sources, showing where major sources cluster onto small residential areas.
harm_angle: A ZIP with several major sources gives residents a cumulative dose no single permit ever evaluated.
caveat: ZIP codes are stored as text and may include plus-four suffixes that split the same ZIP.

title: Which Industries Run The Violators
idea: Ranked bars of NAICS codes by share of their air facilities carrying a current HPV flag, exposing the industries that violate most often.
harm_angle: Naming the sector shows this is a business model, not a run of bad luck at one plant.
caveat: naics_codes appears to hold multiple codes in one string and needs splitting.

title: Local Control Region Patchwork
idea: Map of local control regions colored by facility count and HPV share, showing which local air districts have the heaviest load and the worst compliance.
harm_angle: A weak or overloaded local air district is why a violation next door goes unaddressed for years.
caveat: Local control region fields are likely populated only in a few states like California.

title: Shut Down But Still Listed
idea: Ranked bars by state of facilities whose operating status says closed or shut down while still carrying active program links, exposing zombie records in the enforcement system.
harm_angle: Zombie records let a still-operating site hide behind a closed status and skip inspections.
caveat: Status codes are undocumented in the model; closed status is often simply accurate.

title: Inspection Deserts
idea: Map by state of facilities with no compliance evaluation recorded in recent years, showing where the inspector never shows up.
harm_angle: An uninspected plant is one where a violation simply never gets found, no matter what it is doing.
caveat: Absence of a row is not proof of no inspection -- state-run programs may report inconsistently.

title: State Versus Federal Inspectors
idea: Timeline of evaluation counts split by whether the state or EPA conducted them, showing the handoff of enforcement to states over the years.
harm_angle: Where enforcement moved to states with weak capacity, the people living nearby lost their referee.
caveat: actual_end_date may be text; parsing behavior unverified in this model.

title: Full Versus Partial Evaluations
idea: Ranked bars of states by the share of compliance evaluations that were partial rather than full, showing where the inspection is a look rather than an audit.
harm_angle: A partial evaluation can be checked off as an inspection while missing the process actually harming people.
caveat: Full versus partial is a defined program distinction with legitimate uses; framing needs care.

title: Inspection Interval Distribution
idea: Distribution of the gap in years between consecutive evaluations at the same facility, showing the long tail of sites that go many years unvisited.
harm_angle: A ten-year inspection gap is ten years of unchecked emissions on a community.
caveat: Requires reliable date parsing and full history; a truncated load would fabricate long gaps.

title: The Zero Dollar Penalty
idea: Distribution of penalty amounts on formal enforcement actions with the zero and near-zero bucket highlighted, showing how often serious action carries no financial cost.
harm_angle: A penalty of nothing tells a polluter the cheapest path is to keep polluting.
caveat: Zero can mean 'not yet assessed' rather than 'waived'; needs the enforcement type to disambiguate.

title: Penalty Severity By State
idea: Map by state of median penalty per formal action, showing where breaking air law is cheap and where it is not.
harm_angle: Identical violations priced differently by state means one community's air is legally worth less.
caveat: State attribution comes from the state/EPA flag plus the facility table; not directly in this table.

title: Repeat Offenders Never Punished Harder
idea: Scatter of a facility's cumulative number of formal actions against the penalty on its most recent one, testing whether repeat offending ever escalates the cost.
harm_angle: If penalties never escalate, a repeat polluter has learned that harm is a fixed, affordable line item.
caveat: Requires full enforcement history; a partial load would fabricate first-offender status.

title: Enforcement Over The Years
idea: Timeline of formal action counts and total penalty dollars by settlement year split by state versus federal, showing enforcement rising and collapsing with administrations.
harm_angle: Every trough in the enforcement line is a period when polluters faced no consequence and neighbors faced the pollution.
caveat: Settlement date lags the violation by years, so the timeline shows resolution not offense timing.

title: Which Enforcement Tool Gets Used
idea: Ranked bars of enforcement type descriptions by count and by median penalty, showing which legal tools actually carry teeth and which are paperwork.
harm_angle: When agencies mostly reach for toothless tools, the harm continues while the file shows action taken.
caveat: Enforcement type mix is partly driven by statute, not agency choice.

title: Warning Letters Instead Of Fines
idea: Timeline of informal actions by year and type, showing periods where agencies leaned on letters rather than real enforcement.
harm_angle: A warning letter costs a polluter nothing and buys the neighborhood another year of the same air.
caveat: Formal comparison needs the formal actions table -- this single-source version can only show informal volume.

title: Facilities That Only Ever Get Letters
idea: Ranked bars of facilities by count of informal actions, isolating sites with long informal histories where soft enforcement became the permanent state.
harm_angle: A facility with twenty warning letters and nothing else is a community that has been failed twenty times.
caveat: Informal action counts are not comparable across states with different recording practices.

title: Official Versus Unofficial Actions
idea: Distribution of informal actions by the official flag across states, showing how much enforcement activity is not even formally logged as official.
harm_angle: Unofficial actions leave no record a citizen could ever use to prove a pattern.
caveat: official_flg meaning is undocumented in the model.

title: State Softness Ranked
idea: Ranked bars of states by informal actions per facility, showing which states lean hardest on the no-consequence option.
harm_angle: Living in a letter-writing state means the plant next door will never actually be made to stop.
caveat: Facility denominators must come from the facilities table; this table alone gives counts not rates.

title: What Each Facility Is Permitted To Emit
idea: Ranked bars of pollutants by how many facilities are permitted for them, colored by hazardous class, mapping the permitted chemical universe.
harm_angle: The permitted chemical list is what neighbors are legally allowed to be exposed to and rarely ever see.
caveat: Permitted is not emitted; this table says nothing about actual quantities.

title: Facilities With The Longest Chemical Lists
idea: Distribution of distinct pollutants permitted per facility, naming the sites permitted for dozens of substances at once.
harm_angle: Cumulative exposure to twenty permitted chemicals is never assessed as a whole for the people living beside them.
caveat: Long lists can reflect thorough permitting rather than more emission.

title: Rare Chemicals Rare Oversight
idea: Ranked bars of the pollutants permitted at the fewest facilities, surfacing exotic substances that no broad monitoring program tracks.
harm_angle: A chemical permitted at four sites has four communities exposed and no national study of what it does.
caveat: CAS numbers may be blank for many rows, making chemical identification unreliable.

title: Which Rules Actually Bite
idea: Ranked bars of air program subparts by number of facilities covered, showing which specific rules govern most of the regulated fleet.
harm_angle: Knowing which rule covers the most facilities shows where a single rollback would harm the most people.
caveat: Facility counts here are program-system ids, not necessarily distinct physical sites.

title: Rule Coverage Per Facility
idea: Distribution of how many subparts each facility is subject to, showing sites governed by dozens of rules versus those with almost none.
harm_angle: A large facility subject to very few subparts may have found the classification with the least obligation.
caveat: Subpart applicability depends on process type; low counts are often legitimate.

title: Program To Subpart Structure
idea: Network graph of programs to their subparts sized by facility coverage, a structural map of how air regulation is actually organized.
harm_angle: Seeing the rule structure is how a reader finds which single node protects the most people.
caveat: Five-column bridge table with no dates or geography -- genuinely thin on its own.

title: When Facilities Entered Regulation
idea: Timeline of program begin dates by program type, showing waves of facilities coming under each air rule and the gaps between them.
harm_angle: Facilities that entered regulation late spent those extra years emitting with no rule at all.
caveat: begin_date may be text; parsing unverified in this model.

title: Stale Program Records
idea: Distribution of the gap between a program record's begin date and its last updated date, surfacing entries untouched for decades.
harm_angle: A record nobody has touched in twenty years is a facility nobody has looked at in twenty years.
caveat: Bulk system migrations can reset updated_date en masse, flattening the real staleness signal.

title: Operating Status By Program
idea: Heatmap grid of program against operating status, showing which regulatory programs are full of inactive facilities and which track live ones.
harm_angle: Programs clogged with dead records hide how few live facilities are actually being watched.
caveat: Status codes undocumented in the model.

title: Stack tests over time by outcome
idea: Timeline of completed air stack tests per year split by test status, showing whether smokestack testing has been rising or quietly collapsing.
harm_angle: Fewer stack tests means nobody is checking what neighbors downwind are actually breathing.
caveat: ACTUAL_END_DATE is a try_to_date over a text field; if the raw format is nonstandard the whole time axis nulls out.

title: Who tests: state versus EPA
idea: Small multiples per state of the share of stack tests flagged state-run versus EPA-run, revealing states effectively handed self-policing.
harm_angle: Residents in states where EPA never shows up rely entirely on a regulator that may be captured.
caveat: No state column in this table; state must be derived from the PGM_SYS_ID prefix, which may not be reliable.

title: Pollutants never tested for
idea: Ranked bars of pollutant descriptions by how often they appear in stack tests, with the long tail of rarely-tested pollutants called out.
harm_angle: Pollutants almost never measured are effectively unregulated for the people living beside the stack.
caveat: POLLUTANT_DESCS looks like a packed multi-value string; it needs splitting and the delimiter is unknown.

title: Facilities with long testing gaps
idea: Dot plot of each facility's largest gap between consecutive stack tests, ranked worst first, exposing plants that went years without a measurement.
harm_angle: A plant untested for a decade can emit anything and nobody downwind would know.
caveat: Assumes PGM_SYS_ID is a stable facility id and that dates parse; a facility absent entirely will not appear at all.

title: Self-reported deviations over time
idea: Timeline of Title V compliance certifications split by whether the facility admitted a deviation, showing how often big polluters confess.
harm_angle: If almost nobody self-reports a deviation, the honor-system permit program is not protecting anyone.
caveat: Deviation flag values are uncoded here; blank versus N versus null may be indistinguishable.

title: Never-deviated facilities ranked
idea: Ranked bars of facilities with the most certifications filed and zero admitted deviations, the too-clean-to-be-true list.
harm_angle: Perfect self-reported records at heavy industrial sites suggest the paperwork, not the air, is clean.
caveat: Perfect compliance may be genuine; needs pairing with violation data to mean anything.

title: Certification filing season heatmap
idea: Heatmap grid of certification end dates by month and year, showing bunching and any year the whole program went quiet.
harm_angle: A year where certifications collapse is a year nobody was formally on the hook for their emissions.
caveat: Date parsing risk; bunching may be an artifact of the reporting deadline, not behavior.

title: State versus federal certification review
idea: Slope chart of the state-versus-EPA flag mix at the start and end of the record, showing the drift of oversight away from federal hands.
harm_angle: Handing review to states that lack staff means the certification is a rubber stamp.
caveat: State/EPA flag may describe the data submitter rather than the reviewer.

title: How long violations stay unresolved
idea: Distribution of days between the high-priority-violation day-zero date and the resolution date, by state, exposing where problems fester.
harm_angle: Every unresolved month is another month a neighborhood breathes an illegal amount of pollution.
caveat: Unresolved cases have a null resolution date and would silently drop out, biasing the picture optimistic.

title: Open high-priority violations by state
idea: Map of states shaded by count of air violations with a day-zero date and no resolution date, the still-open harm map.
harm_angle: These are live, admitted violations that the government has not made stop.
caveat: Null resolution date may also mean not-yet-reported rather than genuinely open.

title: Enforcement response policy mix
idea: Ranked bars of enforcement response policy codes by frequency, showing which formal response levels regulators actually reach for.
harm_angle: If the softest response dominates, polluters learn the price of breaking the law is a letter.
caveat: Codes are uncoded here and need a lookup table that may not exist in the warehouse.

title: Pathway to enforcement flow
idea: Flow diagram from violation discovery date through notice-of-violation pathway to resolution, sized by how many cases exit at each step.
harm_angle: Shows the exact stage where enforcement leaks out and polluters walk.
caveat: Pathway date semantics are guessed from column names; the funnel order may be wrong.

title: Repeat air violators cohort grid
idea: Cohort grid of facilities by the year of their first violation, tracking how many keep re-offending in each later year.
harm_angle: Names the plants that treat violations as a cost of doing business.
caveat: Only about 102k rows; cohort cells may be too thin to read for smaller years.

title: Where enforcement cases actually conclude
idea: Map of concluded federal environmental enforcement cases by facility state and city, showing the geography of cases that reached an end.
harm_angle: Places with facilities but no concluded cases are places where breaking the law has no ending.
caveat: No date column in this table, so this is a static snapshot with no trend.

title: Facilities named in the most cases
idea: Ranked bars of facility names appearing in the largest number of distinct concluded enforcement cases.
harm_angle: Repeat defendants show the law is not deterring the biggest actors.
caveat: Facility name matching may split one company across spelling variants; FACILITY_UIN population is unverified.

title: Multi-facility mega-cases
idea: Distribution of how many facilities each concluded case covers, with the long tail of sprawling corporate-wide settlements.
harm_angle: A single settlement covering hundreds of sites can quietly discount per-site accountability.
caveat: Grain assumed one row per case-facility pair; duplicates would inflate the tail.

title: Zip codes carrying repeat cases
idea: Heatmap grid of zip codes by number of concluded-case facilities, surfacing the handful of postcodes that absorb most enforcement.
harm_angle: The same neighborhoods keep hosting the facilities that get sued.
caveat: Zip may be nine-digit or padded inconsistently; needs normalization.

title: Which industries get sued
idea: Ranked bars of primary NAICS codes among facilities named in federal environmental cases, showing the industrial profile of enforcement.
harm_angle: Industries absent from the list may be escaping scrutiny rather than behaving.
caveat: NAICS codes are stored as text and may be blank or ragged in length.

title: Case-facility map by state
idea: Map shaded by count of case facilities per state, as a raw picture of where federal environmental cases land.
harm_angle: States with lots of industry and few cases point to enforcement deserts.
caveat: Raw counts without a denominator of regulated facilities can mislead.

title: Registry-id coverage audit
idea: Ranked bars of the share of case facilities carrying a usable EPA registry id, by state, showing where records cannot be traced to a plant.
harm_angle: Untraceable case records mean the public cannot follow a polluter across programs.
caveat: Registry id may be sentinel-masked rather than null; needs a distinct-value check before trusting.

title: Corporate footprint network
idea: Network of facility names linked by shared case numbers, letting one corporate family light up as a connected cluster.
harm_angle: Reveals that many separate-looking sites are one company facing one bill.
caveat: Name-based clustering is fuzzy; without a parent-company column this may just show noise.

title: Informal actions by statute over time
idea: Timeline of informal EPA enforcement actions split by statute, showing which laws get warnings rather than penalties.
harm_angle: A statute enforced only with warning letters is a law with no teeth for the people it protects.
caveat: Only about 22k rows, so yearly splits by statute may be thin.

title: Warning-letter type mix
idea: Ranked bars of informal enforcement type descriptions, showing what a slap on the wrist actually looks like in practice.
harm_angle: Tells the public exactly how little happens when a polluter is caught.
caveat: Type descriptions may be sparse or inconsistently populated.

title: Facilities that only ever get warnings
idea: Dot plot of facilities by count of informal actions received, highlighting sites with many warnings and no escalation.
harm_angle: Chronic offenders absorbing endless warnings keep polluting the same neighborhood.
caveat: Escalation cannot be proven from this table alone; needs the formal-action tables to confirm no escalation.

title: Federal inspections by region over time
idea: Timeline of EPA inspections per EPA region per year, showing which regions stopped showing up.
harm_angle: An unvisited region is a region where facilities self-regulate by default.
caveat: Dates are try_to_date over text; the coverage window is unknown from metadata.

title: Inspection length distribution
idea: Distribution of inspection duration in days from begin to end date, by statute, showing which laws get a drive-by check.
harm_angle: Fifteen-minute inspections of complex plants are not real oversight.
caveat: Same-day inspections may be genuinely brief or just poorly recorded.

title: Who inspects: agency mix by statute
