caveat: 178M rows means heavy aggregation; needs an external population denominator and the date field cast quality is unverified.

title: Distributor to pharmacy flow
idea: Flow diagram of reporting distributors to buyer types and states for the peak years, showing the handful of firms that moved most of the supply.
harm_angle: Naming the distributors that shipped the flood is naming who profited from the deaths.
caveat: reporter_family grouping quality unverified; corporate name changes split entities.

title: Pharmacies with impossible volume
idea: Scatter of individual buyer pharmacies by annual dosage units against their town's scale, isolating single storefronts that received millions of pills.
harm_angle: A corner pharmacy taking in a million pills a year was a pill mill with a line out the door.
caveat: Chain pharmacies under one DEA number can distort; needs population data not in this table.

title: The supply curve and the cliff
idea: National timeline of morphine-equivalent volume by drug, showing the rise, the peak, and the cliff when the supply was cut.
harm_angle: The cliff is the moment dependent patients were cut off and pushed to street supply.
caveat: Coverage window of the ARCOS pull unverified; the conversion factor may be null for some drugs.

title: Buyer type mix shift by state
idea: Small multiples by state of the share of volume going to pharmacies versus practitioners versus hospitals over time, showing where the pills actually landed.
harm_angle: States where practitioners rather than pharmacies took the volume are states where doctors were dispensing directly.
caveat: Business activity coding unverified; the choice between dosage units and grams changes the picture.

title: Cosmetic Reactions by Product Category
idea: Ranked bars of industry category by number of adverse event reports, split by whether the reported outcome was serious. Shows which shelf of the store generates the injuries.
harm_angle: Consumers get hurt by cosmetics that need no premarket approval at all.
caveat: Outcomes is a nested array; seriousness may need unpacking. Report counts reflect reporting behavior, not incidence.

title: Brands That Keep Coming Back
idea: Dot plot of brand names by report count over time, highlighting brands that produce reports across many years rather than one spike. Persistent brands are the mechanism; one-off spikes are noise.
harm_angle: A brand can generate injury reports for a decade with no recall and no consumer ever seeing the tally.
caveat: Brand strings are free text with spelling variants; naive grouping will fragment the same brand.

title: Reaction Fingerprint by Product Type
idea: Heatmap grid of product category against reaction term, so each category shows its characteristic injury signature such as hair loss for relaxers or burns for peels.
harm_angle: Distinct injury patterns per product type point at specific ingredients hurting specific people.
caveat: Reaction text is MedDRA-coded free text; term sprawl could need heavy grouping.

title: Report Lag From Injury to FDA
idea: Distribution of days between initial received date and latest received date per report, showing how long a case stays open and how often it is revised.
harm_angle: Slow-moving reports mean the warning signal reaches regulators long after the product hurt someone.
caveat: Only captures FDA-side dates; the actual injury date is not in the select list.

title: Who Gets Hurt by Cosmetics
idea: Unpack the patient sub-object into an age-by-sex cohort grid, one cell per demographic, shaded by report rate. Puts a face on the reports.
harm_angle: Shows whether cosmetic injuries land disproportionately on one age or sex group.
caveat: patient is a raw nested object; age and sex fields may be sparse or in unstandardized units.

title: The 510k Firehose Over Time
idea: Timeline of clearances per year split by decision description, showing the volume of devices entering the market through the equivalence shortcut rather than full approval.
harm_angle: Most devices in a patient's body were never independently tested, only declared similar to something older.
caveat: Decision dates are openFDA strings; nulls in early years possible.

title: Review Clock by Specialty
idea: Distribution of days between date received and decision date, small-multipled by advisory committee. Some specialties clear in weeks, others crawl.
harm_angle: Uneven review speed means some patients get devices waved through faster than others.
caveat: Clock stops for FDA information requests are invisible here, so the gap overstates true review effort.

title: Third Party Reviewed Clearances
idea: Ranked bars of applicants by share of their clearances that carry the third-party review flag versus FDA-reviewed. Shows who routes around the agency's own reviewers.
harm_angle: Devices cleared by paid third-party reviewers reach patients without a government scientist ever looking.
caveat: third_party_flag fill rate unverified; may be sparse.

title: Where Device Makers Actually Are
idea: Map applicant address by state and country code, sized by clearance count. Shows the geographic concentration of who supplies American hospitals.
harm_angle: Concentration means a single regional failure can ripple into every hospital in the country.
caveat: Applicant address is the corporate mailing address, not the manufacturing site.

title: Serial Clearers of One Product Code
idea: Ranked bars of product codes by how many distinct applicants have cleared into them and by total clearances. A code with hundreds of clearances is a crowded equivalence chain.
harm_angle: Long equivalence chains let a device drift far from the original tested product with nobody re-testing.
caveat: The actual predicate link is not a column here, so chain depth is inferred from volume, not traced.

title: The Risk Ladder of Device Categories
idea: Ranked bars of medical specialty by count of product codes in each device class, showing which specialties are dominated by high-risk Class III categories.
harm_angle: Patients in some specialties are routinely exposed to the riskiest device tier.
caveat: One row per product code, not per device sold; counts are category counts, not exposure.

title: Implants Exempt From Manufacturing Rules
idea: Cross-tab of implant flag against GMP exempt flag and life-sustaining flag as a heatmap grid. The cell that should be empty — implanted, life-sustaining, and GMP-exempt — is the story.
harm_angle: A device left inside a human body should not be exempt from manufacturing quality rules.
caveat: Flags are strings with blanks; blanks may need to be a visible third state rather than assumed No.

title: Unclassified Device Limbo
idea: Ranked bars of unclassified reasons, showing how many device categories sit outside the risk framework entirely and why.
harm_angle: Devices in classification limbo carry no matched oversight tier.
caveat: unclassified_reason is likely populated on a small subset only.

title: Review Panel Workload Map
idea: Dot plot of review panels by number of product codes owned and share that are Class III, revealing which small panels carry the heaviest risk load.
harm_angle: An overloaded review panel is where inadequate scrutiny becomes systemic.
caveat: Panel size and staffing are not in the data; workload is inferred from category count only.

title: Recall Severity Over Time
idea: Timeline of device recalls per quarter, stacked by classification, so the life-threatening Class I band is visible against the routine ones.
harm_angle: A Class I recall means a device already in use can kill; the trend says whether that is getting worse.
caveat: Recall dates parsed from YYYYMMDD strings; nulls would silently drop from the timeline.

title: Firms With the Longest Recall Rap Sheet
idea: Ranked bars of recalling firms by count of distinct recall events, colored by worst severity ever reached. Names the repeat offenders.
harm_angle: Firms that recall over and over keep selling into hospitals with no escalating consequence visible in the data.
caveat: recalling_firm is free text; subsidiaries and spelling variants will split the same company.

title: Recalls That Never Close
idea: Distribution of days from recall initiation to termination, with still-open recalls shown as an open-ended bar. Exposes recalls that have sat unterminated for years.
harm_angle: An unterminated recall means the defective device may still be in circulation.
caveat: Termination date null could mean open or could mean not-reported; the two are indistinguishable from metadata.

title: Voluntary Versus Ordered Recalls
idea: Slope chart over time of the share of recalls that are firm-initiated versus FDA-mandated, by severity class. Tests whether the agency ever actually orders anything.
harm_angle: If nearly all recalls are voluntary, the enforcement backstop is theoretical.
caveat: voluntary_mandated wording is inconsistent in openFDA and will need grouping.

title: Reason for Recall Themes
idea: Cluster recall reason text into themes and plot theme against device class as a heatmap. Shows whether the killers are software bugs, sterility failures, or labeling.
harm_angle: Naming the recurring failure mode is how you stop the next batch of injuries.
caveat: reason_for_recall is long free text; theming is judgment-heavy and could be criticized as subjective.

title: Supplements Piled on One Approval
idea: Ranked bars of PMA numbers by count of supplements, showing original Class III approvals amended dozens of times without a new full review.
harm_angle: A device changed eighty times since approval is not the device that was tested on patients.
caveat: Supplement types include trivial labeling changes; needs supplement_type filtering to be fair.

title: PMA Approval Time by Applicant
idea: Distribution of days from date received to decision date, small-multipled by the largest applicants. Shows whether big firms get faster answers.
harm_angle: If size buys speed, smaller innovators and the patients waiting on them lose.
caveat: Received-to-decision gap ignores review cycle pauses; applicant names need normalizing.

title: Expedited Review Who Gets It
idea: Ranked bars of applicants and advisory committees by share of PMAs flagged expedited. Shows where the fast lane is used and by whom.
harm_angle: Expedited review trades evidence for speed, and patients carry that trade.
caveat: Flag fill rate unverified; blanks may swamp the Yes values.

title: Class III Device Makers Map
idea: Map applicant state and city, sized by number of PMA approvals held, to show the small set of places that make America's highest-risk devices.
harm_angle: Extreme concentration in high-risk device manufacture is a single point of failure for patients nationwide.
caveat: Corporate address, not plant address.

title: Repeat recalling firms
idea: Ranked bars of firms by number of recalls, split by classification severity, exposing the manufacturers that keep failing.
harm_angle: Firms that recall repeatedly and face no consequence keep shipping unsafe medicine to patients.
caveat: recalling_firm is free text with heavy name variation; counts split across spellings without normalization.

title: How long recalls stay open
idea: Distribution of days from recall initiation to termination by classification, showing how long dangerous product stays in the field.
harm_angle: Every open day on a Class I recall is a day someone can still take the drug.
caveat: termination_date is null for open recalls; those nulls are the worst cases and must not be dropped.

title: Voluntary versus mandated
idea: Timeline of recalls by year split voluntary versus FDA-mandated, showing whether the agency ever forces the issue.
harm_angle: Near-total reliance on voluntary recalls means firms decide when patients learn a drug is unsafe.
caveat: voluntary_mandated is free text with multiple phrasings; needs grouping.

title: Why drugs get recalled
idea: Ranked bars of recall reason categories derived from the reason text, faceted by classification.
harm_angle: Recurring failure modes (contamination, wrong potency) point to a systemic manufacturing problem, not bad luck.
caveat: reason_for_recall is long free text; categorization is judgment work not stored in the table.

title: Distribution reach of the worst recalls
idea: Map of recall firm locations sized by the geographic breadth described in the distribution pattern, focused on Class I events.
harm_angle: Nationwide Class I distribution means the exposed population is everyone, and notification rarely reaches them.
caveat: distribution_pattern is unstructured prose; breadth must be inferred from text.

title: Class I recalls per firm per year
idea: Heatmap grid of firm by year shaded by count of the most severe recall class, isolating chronic offenders.
harm_angle: Chronic Class I offenders are the manufacturers most likely to kill someone next.
caveat: event_id versus recall_number grain unverified; one event may generate many recall numbers and inflate counts.

title: Drug master files filed over time
idea: Timeline of drug master file submissions per year split by active versus inactive status, showing the shape of the ingredient supply chain.
harm_angle: The hidden ingredient suppliers behind every generic drug patients take.
caveat: About 41k rows; the submit date parse depends on the exact text format holding.

title: Biggest ingredient suppliers
idea: Ranked bars of holders by count of active drug master files, naming the companies the whole generic market depends on.
harm_angle: One plant failure at a concentrated supplier creates a national drug shortage.
caveat: Holder is free text with likely name variants; no country column to place them geographically.

title: Inactive file wave
idea: Timeline of the share of files now inactive by original submit year, showing supplier attrition cohorts.
harm_angle: Suppliers going inactive is the leading edge of a drug shortage.
caveat: There is no inactivation-date column, only current status, so the timing of the switch is unknowable.

title: Master file type mix
idea: Ranked bars of file type showing whether filings are ingredients, packaging, or manufacturing sites.
harm_angle: Type tells you which link of the drug supply chain is thinning.
caveat: Type codes are numeric and need an FDA lookup to be readable.

title: Foreign Plants Supplying US Devices
idea: Map registered establishments by country, sized by count and split by establishment type such as manufacturer versus repackager. Shows where devices are actually made versus where the brand lives.
harm_angle: Patients cannot know that a US-branded implant was made in a plant no US inspector has visited.
caveat: One row per registration-product pair, so counts double-count facilities unless deduped on FEI.

title: Owner Operators Behind Many Plants
idea: Network graph of owner operator number linked to the facilities it registers, revealing conglomerates operating under many establishment names.
harm_angle: One owner behind twenty differently-named plants can absorb a scandal at one and keep selling from the rest.
caveat: owner_operator_number populated-ness unverified; a masked or blank id would collapse the graph.

title: Registrations Left to Expire
idea: Timeline of registration expiry year by status code, showing facilities still listing products under lapsed or inactive registration.
harm_angle: A lapsed registration with live product listings means devices shipping outside the tracking system.
caveat: reg_expiry_date_year is a year only; status_code semantics not documented in the model.

title: Establishment Type Supply Chain Flow
idea: Sankey from country of manufacture through establishment type to product listing, tracing how a device moves from foreign maker to US relabeler to market.
harm_angle: Relabeling hides the true maker from anyone trying to hold a manufacturer accountable.
caveat: The flow is inferred from co-registration, not a real chain-of-custody field; it may be a pretty picture with no causal link.

title: Adverse event reports over time
idea: Timeline of adverse event case reports per year split by reporter type, the raw volume of drug harm reaching the FDA.
harm_angle: Every case is a person who was hurt by a medicine.
caveat: Date columns are left uncast as text in the model; 5.8M rows span two id eras that must be reconciled.

title: Who gets hurt: age and sex
idea: Distribution of reported patient age by gender code, showing which bodies show up in the harm data.
harm_angle: Reveals whether drug harm concentrates in the elderly, in women, or in children.
caveat: AGE is uncast text and the age unit code mixes years, months and decades; without normalization the distribution is meaningless.

title: Manufacturer versus consumer reporting
idea: Timeline of the share of reports originating from manufacturers versus consumers and clinicians, showing who does the reporting work.
harm_angle: If only manufacturers report, they control the picture of their own product's harm.
caveat: Reporter code encodings unverified; the two data eras may use different code sets.

title: Reporting delay by manufacturer
idea: Distribution of days from the event date to the FDA receipt date, split by manufacturer sender, exposing slow reporters.
harm_angle: Late reporting delays the safety signal and lets more patients be exposed.
caveat: Date columns are raw text and these dates are notoriously partial (year-only or year-month).

title: Deaths reported by year
idea: Timeline of reports carrying a death date, showing fatal adverse events across the record.
harm_angle: These are deaths the FDA was told about and the public rarely sees counted.
caveat: The death date is uncast text and may be sparsely populated; it overlaps with the outcome table's death code.

title: Case version churn
idea: Distribution of case version numbers per case id, showing which cases were revised many times.
harm_angle: Heavily revised cases can indicate a manufacturer negotiating the record of a harm.
caveat: Case version only exists for the modern-era rows; legacy rows will be blank.

title: Drugs named in the most reports
idea: Ranked bars of drug names by count of adverse event reports where they are the primary suspect.
harm_angle: Names the medicines most often blamed for hurting patients.
caveat: DRUGNAME is free text with massive spelling and brand/generic variation; the catalog row count is missing so table size is unconfirmed.

title: Suspect versus bystander role mix
idea: Ranked bars of drugs by the ratio of primary-suspect to concomitant mentions, isolating drugs usually named as the cause.
harm_angle: A drug almost always named as the suspect is a drug with a real safety problem.
caveat: Role code encoding unverified; free-text drug names need heavy normalization.

title: Stop-and-restart evidence grid
idea: Heatmap grid of drugs against dechallenge and rechallenge outcomes, the closest thing this data has to causal evidence.
harm_angle: A drug that hurts, stops hurting when withdrawn, and hurts again on restart is a proven harm.
caveat: The dechallenge and rechallenge fields are notoriously sparse in this dataset.

title: Dose amount versus report volume
idea: Scatter of reported dose amount against report count per drug, testing whether harm reports cluster at higher doses.
harm_angle: Dose-response patterns in real-world reports can flag labels that permit too much.
caveat: DOSE_AMT is a try_to_double over free text and the dose unit varies wildly; comparability is dubious.

title: Polypharmacy load per case
idea: Distribution of the number of drugs listed per case, showing how many patients were on ten or more medicines.
harm_angle: Heavily medicated patients, mostly elderly, are the population these harms land on hardest.
caveat: The drug sequence numbering may restart per case in inconsistent ways across the two data eras.

title: What the drugs were prescribed for
idea: Ranked bars of indication terms across all adverse event reports, showing the conditions being treated when harm occurred.
harm_angle: Reveals whether harms cluster around conditions where safer alternatives existed.
caveat: 9.8M rows at drug-indication grain; the indication term is a coded medical term needing a dictionary.

title: Off-label harm signal
idea: Heatmap grid of indications against drug, surfacing indications that do not match the approved use.
harm_angle: Off-label prescribing that ends in harm is a mechanism nobody is held accountable for.
caveat: Determining off-label requires an approved-indication reference this table does not contain.

title: Indications with the most reports over time
idea: Timeline of report counts for the top indication terms by source quarter, showing which treatment areas generate harm signals.
harm_angle: Rising harm in one treatment area points at a class of drugs failing patients.
caveat: The source quarter is a loader field and may not cleanly represent the report date.

title: Outcome severity mix over time
idea: Timeline of adverse event outcomes by code (death, hospitalization, disability, life-threatening) per source quarter.
harm_angle: Shows whether the harm reaching the FDA is getting more severe.
caveat: Two outcome columns exist for the two data eras and must be unioned; code encoding needs a lookup.

title: Cases with multiple severe outcomes
idea: Distribution of the count of distinct outcome codes per case, isolating the catastrophic multi-outcome cases.
harm_angle: Cases carrying death plus disability plus hospitalization are the worst individual harms in the file.
caveat: Grain is assumed one row per case-outcome pair; duplicates across quarters would inflate counts.

title: Death share of all reports
idea: Timeline of the share of cases carrying a death outcome, the single hardest number in the adverse event system.
harm_angle: The death share is the clearest measure of how badly medicines are hurting people.
caveat: Reporting behavior changes over time, so a rising share may reflect reporting rather than risk.

title: Most reported adverse reactions
idea: Ranked bars of reaction terms across all reports, the plain list of what happens to people.
harm_angle: Names the actual bodily harms patients experience.
caveat: The reaction term is a coded medical dictionary entry; readability needs a term hierarchy.

title: Reaction co-occurrence network
idea: Network of reaction terms linked when they appear in the same case, revealing recognizable syndromes emerging from the noise.
harm_angle: Clusters of co-reported reactions can be an unnamed syndrome nobody has flagged yet.
caveat: Very large table; co-occurrence needs aggressive thresholding or it becomes a hairball.

title: Emerging reaction terms
idea: Timeline of the fastest-rising reaction terms by source quarter, a signal-detection view of new harms appearing.
harm_angle: A reaction term that suddenly spikes is often a new harm before anyone announces it.
caveat: The source quarter reflects the data drop, not necessarily when the event occurred.

title: Devices Pulled From Distribution
idea: Timeline of commercial distribution status by year, showing how many device identifiers have quietly exited the market versus how many entered.
harm_angle: A device silently leaving the market with no recall notice leaves patients with an unsupported implant.
caveat: 5M rows at device-identifier grain; publish_date may reflect database entry rather than market entry.

title: The Labelers Behind Every Brand
idea: Ranked bars of labeler DUNS numbers by count of distinct brand names they publish, exposing how few companies stand behind thousands of brand fronts.
harm_angle: Brand proliferation makes it near-impossible for a patient to know who actually made their device.
caveat: labeler_duns_number could be sparsely populated or sentinel-filled; check distinct count before trusting it as a key.

title: Combination Products and Kits
idea: Cross-tab of kit flag against combination-product flag by primary product code as a heatmap. Combination products straddle drug and device rules and often fall between them.
harm_angle: Products that straddle two regulatory regimes are where oversight gaps live.
caveat: Boolean-ish string fields; blank handling changes the picture.

title: Model Number Sprawl Per Device
idea: Distribution of how many version and catalog numbers share a single product code per company. Sprawl is a tracking hazard when a recall lands.
harm_angle: When one product code carries hundreds of model numbers, a recall notice cannot reach the right patients.
caveat: Model and catalog strings are free text and may include junk values.

title: Deaths Injuries and Malfunctions Over Time
idea: Timeline of adverse event reports by month split by event type, so death reports are visible against the malfunction background.
harm_angle: These are people injured or killed by devices already on the market.
caveat: Coverage is 2020Q1-forward only per the model comment; earlier history is not landed and any trend claim must say so.

title: Manufacturers With the Most Death Reports
idea: Ranked bars of manufacturer by count of death-type reports, normalized against their total reports so raw volume alone does not top the chart.
harm_angle: Names the makers whose devices show up most often when someone dies.
caveat: Manufacturer names are free text with heavy variant sprawl; manufacturer_name and manufacturer_d_name may disagree.

title: Reporting Delay From Event to FDA
idea: Distribution of days between date of event and date received, split by manufacturer. Long tails are firms sitting on bad news.
harm_angle: Every month of delay is another month of the same device hurting the next patient.
caveat: Raw date fields sit alongside parsed ones, hinting at parse failures; trimming absurd gaps can hide the worst cases.

title: Where Device Makers Report From
idea: Map manufacturer country and state shaded by death-report share, testing whether offshore manufacture correlates with worse reported outcomes.
harm_angle: If offshore plants generate a higher death share, the inspection gap has a body count.
caveat: Manufacturer address is the reporting address; correlation is not causation and reporting practices differ by country.

title: One Device Code One Long Story
idea: Small multiples per device report product code of monthly report counts, so a viewer can spot codes with a sudden sustained step change — the signature of a bad lot or design change.
harm_angle: A step change nobody acted on is exactly where a preventable injury pattern hides.
caveat: Reporting volume responds to publicity as much as to failures; a step could be a lawsuit, not a defect.

title: Biologic Exclusivity Wall Timeline
idea: Plot each biologic license as a horizontal bar from approval date to exclusivity expiration, grouped by applicant, to see how long each maker holds the market closed.
harm_angle: Patients pay brand prices for as long as the exclusivity wall stands and this shows who holds the longest walls.
caveat: Two-digit source years make pre-1970 dates century-ambiguous; exclusivity dates may be sparsely populated.

title: Who Owns The Biologics
idea: Ranked bars of applicants by count of distinct BLA numbers and products, split by license type (original vs biosimilar).
harm_angle: Concentration of biologic licensing in a few firms is the upstream cause of drug prices patients cannot pay.
caveat: Applicant names are free text; the same company may appear under several spellings.

title: Biosimilar Gap After Reference Approval
idea: Scatter of reference-product approval date against the first biosimilar approval date for the same proper name showing years of monopoly per molecule.
harm_angle: Every year between the original and its first competitor is a year of unchallenged pricing paid by patients.
caveat: Requires the reference-product linkage columns to be populated; unverified.

title: Interchangeability Rarely Granted
idea: Small multiples by dosage form showing the share of products that ever received an interchangeable approval date versus those that never did.
harm_angle: Without interchangeability a pharmacist cannot substitute, so patients keep paying the brand price.
caveat: Interchangeable date may be almost entirely null, collapsing the chart.

title: Orphan Status As A Shield
idea: Dot plot comparing orphan exclusivity expiration against ordinary exclusivity expiration per product to spot molecules stacking orphan protection on top of standard protection.
harm_angle: Rare-disease incentives meant to help small patient groups can be stacked to extend monopolies.
caveat: Orphan date column may be very thinly populated.

title: Substance Crosswalk Completeness Grid
idea: Heatmap grid of substance type against each external identifier (CAS, RXCUI, PubChem, EPA CompTox, ITIS) showing which classes of substance are well cross-referenced and which are dark.
harm_angle: Substances with no crosswalk cannot be tracked from a drug label to an environmental release, so harm goes unlinked.
caveat: Identifier columns may hold blanks rather than nulls; needs distinct-value checks before trusting.

title: Substances With No Chemical Structure
idea: Ranked bars of ingredient type by share of records missing both molecular formula and InChIKey exposing the ingredient classes registered as names only.
harm_angle: An ingredient with no structure recorded cannot be matched to a toxicity study, so its risk is invisible.
caveat: Structureless entries may be legitimately non-chemical (proteins, mixtures).

title: Registry Composition By Substance Type
idea: Distribution of the registry across substance type and ingredient type as a ranked breakdown of what the registry actually contains.
harm_angle: Baseline showing how much of the chemical universe regulators have even bothered to name.

title: The Chemical Biological Bridge Network
idea: Network where a substance is a node and each populated crosswalk (CAS, ITIS, NCBI, USDA Plants, PubChem) is an edge to that registry, revealing which registries actually touch each other.
harm_angle: Shows where the public record is stitched together and where it is severed which decides what harms can be traced.
caveat: Network may be dominated by one hub registry and read as a hairball.

source_names: HHS OIG List of Excluded Individuals and Entities
title: Exclusions over time by type
idea: Timeline of exclusions by exclusion type to show which conduct categories drive federal healthcare bans and how enforcement volume shifted.
harm_angle: Exclusion is the strongest consumer protection in healthcare and its volume shows how often it is actually used.
caveat: Exclusion date may be a text or YYYYMMDD field vulnerable to the epoch-cast trap.

source_names: HHS OIG List of Excluded Individuals and Entities
title: Exclusions per capita by state
idea: Map of states by exclusions per thousand providers to show whether enforcement intensity varies wildly by geography.
harm_angle: If two identical bad actors in different states face different odds of being excluded then enforcement itself is the inequity.
caveat: Needs a provider-count denominator from another source; state field is the excluded party's address.

source_names: HHS OIG List of Excluded Individuals and Entities
title: Excluded specialties ranked
idea: Ranked bars of specialty by exclusion count normalised by how common the specialty is to show which corners of medicine produce the most bans.
harm_angle: Specialties producing disproportionate exclusions are where patients most need to check a provider before their first visit.
caveat: Specialty text is inconsistent and often blank for entities.

source_names: HHS OIG List of Excluded Individuals and Entities
title: Reinstatement rates by exclusion type
idea: Slope or dot plot of the share reinstated by exclusion type and exclusion year to show which bans are permanent and which are a pause.
harm_angle: Providers reinstated after patient-harm exclusions return to treating the same population.
caveat: was_reinstated derivation unverified; the LEIE snapshot may drop reinstated parties entirely.

source_names: HHS OIG List of Excluded Individuals and Entities
title: Excluded entities without an NPI
idea: Grid or bars showing what share of exclusions carry a usable NPI split by individual versus entity to quantify how untraceable the ban list is.
harm_angle: An exclusion with no identifier cannot be enforced at the billing system so the excluded party keeps working.
caveat: NPI in LEIE is known to be sparsely populated and needs a distinct-value check before trusting.

title: Doctor Shortage Severity Map
idea: County map of primary-care shortage scores with the highest-severity shortage areas driven to the front.
harm_angle: A high shortage score means residents there physically cannot get a primary care appointment.
caveat: Multiple shortage components can cover the same county so deduplication is needed.

title: Shortage Designations Never Updated
idea: Distribution of years since the last designation update by state showing designations running on stale data.
harm_angle: A stale designation means either unearned federal money or unrecognized worsening shortage.
caveat: Withdrawn designations must be excluded or they distort the distribution.

title: Underserved Population Versus Provider Goal
idea: Scatter of estimated underserved population against the provider ratio goal and current ratio sized by designation population.
harm_angle: The gap between the ratio goal and reality is the number of people with no doctor.
caveat: Ratio fields may be text; provider FTE may be zero for many components.

title: Rural Versus Metro Shortage
idea: Small multiples comparing shortage score distributions across rural status and metropolitan indicator categories.
harm_angle: Rural residents facing higher shortage scores means longer drives and later diagnoses.
caveat: Rural status coding may have several categories needing grouping.

title: Poverty And The Shortage Score
idea: Scatter of percentage of population below poverty against shortage score colored by population type testing whether shortage tracks poverty.
harm_angle: Where poverty and provider shortage stack, people get sicker before they ever see a doctor.
caveat: Poverty percentage may be a designation input rather than independent evidence.

title: Designations Withdrawn Over Time
idea: Timeline of withdrawal events by state showing which states lost shortage designations and therefore lost federal placement help.
harm_angle: A withdrawn designation ends the federal incentives that were the only thing bringing doctors in.
caveat: Withdrawn date exists as both a date and a string column, suggesting parse problems.

title: Border Counties Shortage Cluster
idea: Map focused on border counties comparing shortage scores against non-border counties in the same states.
harm_angle: Border communities carry both the highest shortage and the least political attention.
caveat: Border indicator population unverified.

title: Malpractice Payments Over Two Decades
idea: Timeline of total malpractice payment amounts and payment counts by report year split by practitioner type.
harm_angle: Baseline of how much harm is being paid for and by whom.
caveat: This dataset is deliberately de-identified so practitioner identity is not recoverable.

title: Repeat Offenders Never Disciplined
idea: Scatter of prior malpractice report count against prior license or clinical privilege action count per practitioner record showing the quadrant of many payouts and zero discipline.
harm_angle: Practitioners with a stack of paid claims and no license action keep treating patients.
caveat: Prior-report counts are as-of-report snapshots so interpretation needs care.

title: State Discipline Rate Disparity
idea: State map of adverse actions per malpractice payment exposing states that pay claims but rarely discipline.
harm_angle: Patients in states that never discipline are exposed to practitioners other states would have stopped.
caveat: State fields may be masked to protect identity in low-count states.

title: Who The Patients Were
idea: Heatmap grid of patient age band against patient sex and allegation nature weighted by payment amount.
harm_angle: Puts the actual injured people, by age and sex, at the center of the malpractice record.
caveat: Age is banded; allegation codes need the source codebook.

title: Payment Size By Allegation Type
idea: Distribution of payment amounts by allegation nature showing which categories of harm are valued highest and lowest.
harm_angle: How much a life-altering outcome is worth in dollars, by category of error.
caveat: Payment amounts may be banded rather than exact in the public-use file.

title: Time From Incident To Payment
idea: Distribution of years between the malpractice year and the report year by practitioner type and state.
harm_angle: Years between the injury and any payment is time the patient spent uncompensated.
caveat: Year fields may be banded or masked.

title: Adverse Action Length Distribution
idea: Distribution of adverse action lengths by action class showing whether discipline is a slap or a stop.
harm_angle: Thirty-day suspensions for serious harm mean the practitioner is back with the same patients next month.
caveat: Length type units vary (days, months, indefinite) and need normalizing.

title: Shortage severity map
idea: Map of HPSA designations coloured by HPSA score and split by discipline (primary care dental mental health) to show the depth of the gap not just its presence.
harm_angle: A high-score shortage area is a place where getting a doctor's appointment is functionally impossible.
caveat: 165k rows include withdrawn and proposed designations that must be filtered by status.

title: Decades-long designations
idea: Distribution of how long each designation has been in place to show shortage areas that have been officially recognised as underserved for thirty years and never fixed.
harm_angle: A place designated a shortage area since the 1970s is a place the country decided not to fix.
caveat: Designation date may be re-stamped on each review which would collapse the apparent duration.

title: Underserved population count ranked
idea: Ranked bars of designations by estimated underserved population showing where the largest number of actual people go without care.
harm_angle: Ranking by people rather than by place puts urban shortage areas back in a conversation dominated by rural ones.
caveat: Served and underserved population estimates are formula-derived not counted.

title: Poverty and shortage together
idea: Scatter of the percent of population below poverty against the HPSA score to show that the deepest care shortages sit on the poorest populations.
harm_angle: The people least able to pay for care out of pocket are the people with the fewest providers to pay.
caveat: Poverty column name is mangled in the mart which suggests a header parsing problem.

title: Mental health shortage versus primary care
idea: Small multiples per state of the count of designations by discipline to show states where mental health shortage is universal while primary care is fine.
harm_angle: Someone in crisis in a mental-health-only shortage state has a family doctor and no psychiatrist to refer them to.
caveat: Discipline class vocabulary unverified.

title: Border county care gap
idea: Map of the US-Mexico border corridor showing HPSA scores and provider ratio goals in the hundred-kilometre border zone.
harm_angle: Border communities combine the worst provider ratios with the largest uninsured population in the country.
caveat: Border indicator flags may be sparsely set.

title: Funding Streams Behind Each Center
idea: Stacked ranked bars of health centers by their four funding streams — community, migrant and seasonal, homeless, public housing — showing which populations each center is actually funded to serve.
harm_angle: Special-population funding is the only reason care exists for migrant workers and homeless patients in many counties.
caveat: The model does not say whether the funding fields are flags or dollar amounts; 1356 rows suggests a single reporting year.

title: Rural Versus Urban Health Center Map
idea: Map of health centers by city and state colored by the urban-rural flag, against a backdrop of state population. Shows the rural centers standing alone.
harm_angle: A rural county with one funded health center has one point of failure for everyone's primary care.
caveat: Address is the administrative grantee site, not every service delivery site; one grantee may run twenty clinics from one address.

title: Special Population Funding by State
idea: Heatmap grid of state against the four funding types shaded by count of centers, exposing states with zero homeless-population funded centers.
harm_angle: An empty cell is a state where a whole vulnerable population has no dedicated funded care.
caveat: Funding field semantics unconfirmed; a zero could mean unfunded or simply unreported.

title: Safety Net Clinics On The Map
idea: Point map of every federally qualified health center delivery site colored by site status and sized by operating hours.
harm_angle: Where the safety net physically exists, and where the map is empty.
caveat: Site status includes inactive sites which must be filtered out.

title: Clinic Hours Per County
idea: County map of total weekly clinic hours per capita across safety-net sites revealing counties with clinics that are barely open.
harm_angle: A clinic open eight hours a week is a clinic most working people cannot use.
caveat: Requires external population data; operating hours may be unreliable self-reports.

title: Clinics By Congressional District
idea: Ranked bars of safety-net site counts and hours per congressional district named by the sitting representative.
harm_angle: Ties safety-net coverage directly to the members of Congress who vote on its funding.
caveat: Representative names in the file are as-of-ingest and go stale each election.

title: Site Types And Settings
idea: Distribution of sites by location setting and site type showing how much of the safety net is mobile, school-based or seasonal.
harm_angle: Seasonal and mobile sites mean intermittent care for the people least able to travel.
caveat: Descriptive code fields may have many overlapping categories.

title: Safety Net Expansion Timeline
idea: Timeline of sites added to scope by year and region showing where the network grew and where it stalled.
harm_angle: Regions where the safety net stopped growing are where unmet need has been accumulating.
caveat: Added-to-scope date may be missing for older sites.

title: Border Clinic Coverage
idea: Map of border-indicator sites against non-border sites within the same states comparing density and hours.
harm_angle: Border communities depend disproportionately on these clinics and thin coverage there has no fallback.
caveat: Border indicator population unverified.

title: Patient Age and Sex Pyramid Per Center
idea: Population pyramid built from the paired male and female line columns by age band, small-multipled for the largest centers.
harm_angle: Who a safety-net clinic actually serves determines which services it must have and often does not.
caveat: Columns are opaque line numbers with no labels in the model — the age-band mapping must come from the UDS manual or the whole idea collapses.

title: Children as a Share of Safety Net Patients
idea: Ranked bars of health centers by the share of patients in the child age bands, showing which centers are effectively pediatric practices.
harm_angle: Centers serving mostly children need pediatric capacity their funding formula may not reflect.
caveat: Same unlabeled-column problem; also only 1356 rows, likely a single year.

title: Elderly Concentration in Health Centers
idea: Dot plot of centers by share of patients in the oldest age bands, rolled up to state as a choropleth using the center info sheet's geography.
harm_angle: Aging patient bases in safety-net clinics signal communities where nobody else is left to provide care.
caveat: Assumes the highest line numbers are the oldest age bands — an unverified guess from the column naming alone.

title: Indian Health Service Coverage Map
idea: Point map of facilities colored by whether they are federally operated, tribally operated or urban programs, sized by bed count.
harm_angle: Where the only health system available to tribal citizens physically exists.
caveat: Bed count may be zero for clinics; only 1,006 rows.

title: Services Missing By Area
idea: Heatmap grid of service area against the presence of behavioral health, dental and pharmacy services.
harm_angle: An area with no behavioral health facility means tribal citizens in crisis have nowhere to go.
caveat: Service flags may be inconsistently maintained.

title: Beds Per Area
idea: Ranked bars of service areas by total bed count and facility count with the missing population denominator flagged.
harm_angle: Areas with almost no inpatient beds send patients hundreds of miles for care.
caveat: Requires external service-population data to normalize; not present here.

title: Tribal Versus Federal Operation
idea: Distribution of facilities by operator and owner type showing how much of the system has been handed to tribes to run.
harm_angle: Handing operations to tribes without matching funding transfers the burden, not the resources.
caveat: No time axis in the table, so the shift cannot actually be shown over time.

title: Service Unit Facility Inventory
idea: Ranked bars of service units by facility count and bed count drilling from area down to service unit.
harm_angle: Service units with almost no facilities are the tribal communities furthest from care.
caveat: 8,733 rows against 1,006 in the main facility table suggests a different grain, possibly multi-year; unverified.

title: Facility Status Across Areas
idea: Heatmap grid of area against facility status and location type showing closed or inactive facilities by region.
harm_angle: A closed facility in a remote service unit removes the only care within a day's drive.
caveat: Status vocabulary unverified; the grain of this table is unclear.

title: Facility Category Breakdown
idea: Distribution of facilities by operating category (federal, tribal, urban) within each service area.
harm_angle: Urban Indian programs serve the majority of Native people but hold the smallest share of facilities.
caveat: Thin table with only ten columns and no dates or geography.

title: Drug Label Revision Churn
idea: Distribution of drug label set ids by version number, exposing the labels that have been rewritten dozens of times.
harm_angle: A label rewritten thirty times is usually a drug whose safety picture kept changing under patients already taking it.
caveat: Only the current version per set id is stored (grain is one row per set id), so this shows a snapshot of version counters, not full revision history.

title: Label Upload Timeline
idea: Timeline of label uploads by month, showing surges that usually follow regulatory actions or mass relabeling events.
harm_angle: Upload surges mark moments when many drugs changed their warnings at once, which patients rarely hear about.
caveat: upload_date is text-cast to date and may fail for a share of rows; upload date is not the same as effective date.

title: High Version Old Upload Quadrant
idea: Scatter of label version number against last upload date, isolating heavily-revised labels that then went years without an update.
harm_angle: A drug with a volatile safety history whose label then froze is a drug whose warnings may now be out of date.
caveat: Version numbering conventions may differ between manufacturers, so version count is not directly comparable across products.

title: Reported versus expected staffing gap
idea: Ranked bars of facilities by the deviation between reported and expected nurse staffing hours to name the homes furthest below what their residents' acuity requires.
harm_angle: The expected-hours benchmark is the honest one because it accounts for how sick the residents actually are.
caveat: This source overlaps heavily with the CMS nursing home file; the expected-hours columns are LTCCC's addition.

title: Problem facilities and their chains
idea: Map of facilities flagged as special focus candidates or one-star coloured by chain to show whether the worst homes cluster under specific owners.
harm_angle: Residents in a chain's worst buildings are living the outcome of a corporate staffing policy not a local failure.
caveat: Chain name normalisation is required; latitude and longitude may be blank for some facilities.

title: Complaints versus fines
idea: Scatter of substantiated complaints against total fine dollars to find facilities with many upheld complaints and almost no financial penalty.
harm_angle: When upheld complaints do not translate into penalties the complaint process is a suggestion box.
caveat: Column is 'total_number_of_penalties' in the model; complaint counts are cycle-scoped.

title: RN staffing deviation by ownership
idea: Distribution of the deviation from expected RN staffing split by detailed ownership type to test whether for-profit and private-equity-style owners cut the most skilled staff.
harm_angle: Registered nurses are the staff who catch a decline before it becomes a hospitalisation and they are the first cut.
caveat: ownership_type_detail granularity unverified; may be as coarse as the CMS field.

title: Turnover and inspection score
idea: Scatter of total nursing staff turnover against the health deficiency count with administrator departures sized to show instability driving citations.
harm_angle: Residents in a home with total staff churn are cared for by people who have never met them.
caveat: Turnover is annualised while deficiencies are cycle-based.

title: Veteran versus non-veteran cause mix
idea: Small multiples by cause of death comparing the age-adjusted rate across veteran cohorts and sex to show where veterans die at higher rates than the general population.
harm_angle: Causes where veterans die faster point at what military service or VA care did to them.
caveat: Whether a non-veteran comparison cohort is present in the cohort column is unverified.

title: Years of life lost by cause
idea: Ranked bars of causes by years of potential life lost rather than raw deaths to show which causes steal the most veteran life-years.
harm_angle: Ranking by life-years lost puts suicide and overdose above heart disease and changes where the money should go.
caveat: Only 2808 rows across six years so cohort granularity is coarse.

title: Cause ranking churn 2018 to 2023
idea: Slope chart of each cause's rank across the six years showing causes climbing the leaderboard including any pandemic-era shifts.
harm_angle: A cause climbing the veteran death ranking is a system failure that has not yet been named.
caveat: Rank is within cohort-sex so mixing groups scrambles the chart.

title: Male versus female veteran divergence
idea: Dot plot of age-adjusted rate by cause with male and female veterans side by side to show where women veterans are worse off.
harm_angle: Women veterans are a small share of the population and their excess mortality gets averaged away in headline VA numbers.
caveat: Small female counts may be suppressed or unstable.

source_names: VA National Veteran Suicide Data Appendix
title: Veteran suicide rate by sex over time
idea: Timeline of unadjusted and age-adjusted veteran suicide rates by sex from 2001 forward with the divergence between the two lines called out.
harm_angle: Veteran suicide is the clearest measure of whether the country's care for the people it sent to war is working.
caveat: The mart is 144 rows of unnamed COL_1 through COL_12 — the spreadsheet headers were never parsed so every field needs manual identification before any chart is possible.

source_names: VA National Veteran Suicide Data Appendix
title: Adjusted versus unadjusted gap
idea: Slope chart of the unadjusted and age-adjusted rate per year to show how much of the apparent trend is just the veteran population getting older.
harm_angle: If the headline rate is falling only because of ageing then prevention is not actually working.
caveat: Same unparsed-header problem; column meanings are unknown from metadata alone.

title: Canada's drug catalogue by class
idea: Ranked bars of approved drug products by drug class, the plain shape of what Health Canada has licensed.
harm_angle: Reference floor for any later question about which drugs are and are not available on which side of the border.
caveat: Loader defect: the first data row was eaten as the header and columns were renamed positionally, so one record is missing and field alignment should be spot-checked.

title: Same molecule many brands
idea: Ranked bars of active-ingredient groups by how many distinct branded products share them, showing where the same chemistry is sold under a dozen names.
harm_angle: Brand proliferation over identical chemistry is how price differences survive; patients pay for the label.
caveat: AI_GROUP_NO population unverified; positional renaming means this column's identity should be confirmed against the DPD layout.

title: Combination-drug complexity
idea: Distribution of number of active ingredients per product, split by class, showing where the market runs on single molecules versus stacked combinations.
harm_angle: Multi-ingredient products are harder for patients and prescribers to reason about and to substitute cheaply.
caveat: Positional column rename risk applies; number_of_ais parsed from text.

title: Records nobody has touched in years
idea: Timeline of last-update dates across the catalogue, exposing the products whose registry entry has gone stale.
harm_angle: A stale registry entry for a drug still on shelves means the public safety record is out of date for a product people are swallowing.
caveat: Date parsed with a fixed DD-MON-YYYY format; other formats become null and would look like missing rather than stale.

title: Listings over four decades
idea: Timeline of chemical listings by date listed and toxicity type showing the pace of California adding cancer and reproductive toxicants.
harm_angle: Every year a chemical sits unlisted is a year of exposure with no warning label.
caveat: Only 952 rows; date_listed may be text.

title: How chemicals get listed
idea: Ranked bars of listing mechanism (authoritative body state qualified experts labor code) to show which pathway actually produces listings and which is dormant.
harm_angle: A dormant listing pathway means a whole category of evidence never reaches a warning label.
caveat: Mechanism vocabulary unverified.

title: Chemicals with no safe-harbour level
idea: Ranked or grid view of listed chemicals lacking an NSRL or MADL safe-harbour number to show where the law gives no usable exposure threshold.
harm_angle: Without a safe-harbour level businesses either over-warn or ignore the listing entirely and consumers learn nothing.
caveat: The safe-harbour column may be mostly blank which is itself the finding but makes a chart thin.

title: Cancer versus reproductive toxicity split
idea: Distribution of listings by toxicity type over time showing whether reproductive toxicants are listed at a fraction of the rate of carcinogens.
harm_angle: Under-listing reproductive toxicants means pregnant workers and consumers get no warning about the exposures that harm a fetus.
caveat: Three chemicals span multiple toxicity types so row grain double-counts them.

title: Abortion counts before and after bans
idea: Timeline of monthly abortion provision by state with ban effective dates marked to show volume collapsing in some states and surging in neighbours.
harm_angle: Where provision collapsed people carried pregnancies they did not choose or travelled hundreds of miles.
caveat: Ban dates are not in this source and would have to be added by hand; month may be text.

title: Estimate uncertainty by state
idea: Timeline per state of the median with the lower and upper bound band shaded to show which states' numbers are near-guesses.
harm_angle: Where the estimate is wide nobody actually knows how many people are getting care and policy is made blind.
caveat: Bound columns may be null for some states.

title: Receiving states absorbed the demand
idea: Ranked bars of states by percentage increase in monthly provision since the series start to identify the states carrying displaced patients.
harm_angle: Clinics in receiving states have waiting lists that push everyone's care later into pregnancy including their own residents.
caveat: Series start date and length unverified from metadata.

title: Revision history of published estimates
idea: Small multiples showing how a given state-month estimate changed across publish dates to reveal how much the public number moved after the fact.
harm_angle: Numbers quoted in court and legislature debates were later revised and nobody went back to correct the record.
caveat: Requires multiple publishdate versions of the same state-month which may not be retained.

title: US against its peer countries
idea: Timeline of life expectancy for the US alongside comparable rich countries showing the divergence that opened after the 1980s.
harm_angle: Americans die years earlier than people in equally rich countries and that gap is a policy choice.
caveat: Entity list mixes countries regions and aggregates so filtering by code is needed.

title: Countries that went backwards
idea: Ranked bars of countries by the largest drop in life expectancy from their own historical peak to identify reversals not just slow growth.
harm_angle: A country whose life expectancy fell had a system collapse and the people who died are the receipt.
caveat: War and pandemic years dominate; needs care not to just rediscover 2020.

title: Convergence or divergence globally
idea: Distribution of country life expectancy per decade to show whether the world's health gap is narrowing or splitting into two groups.
harm_angle: A widening global distribution means being born in the wrong country costs decades of life.
caveat: Unweighted by population so small countries dominate the shape.

title: Two hundred years in one grid
idea: Heatmap of country by year coloured by life expectancy sorted by current value to show the whole modern history of who lived long and when.
harm_angle: The grid makes visible how recently and unevenly long life arrived for most of the world.
caveat: Sparse early years for most countries will leave large blank regions.

title: Veteran Versus Civilian Suicide Gap
idea: Timeline of age-adjusted suicide rates for veterans, VHA users, non-veterans and all US adults, 2001-2023, on one panel.
harm_angle: The gap between veterans and civilians is the measurable cost of how service members are treated after service.
caveat: Rates are published; comparability depends on VA methodology changes mid-series.

title: Does VA Care Change The Rate
idea: Slope chart comparing VHA-user and other-veteran rates at each year end, showing whether being inside the system helps.
harm_angle: If VHA users fare no better, the care system is not reaching the people at risk.
caveat: VHA users are a selected, sicker population, so the comparison is confounded and not causal.

title: Women Veterans Rate Curve
idea: Timeline of female versus male veteran rates indexed to their civilian counterparts, showing the relative burden on women veterans.
harm_angle: Women veterans relative excess risk is routinely buried inside the male-dominated total.
caveat: Female counts are small, so rates may be unstable or suppressed in some years.

title: Age Cohorts Moving Apart
idea: Small multiples of unadjusted rate by age group over time, showing whether the youngest or oldest veterans drive the trend.
harm_angle: Knowing which age band is worsening tells you which policy era failed them.
caveat: Age-group rows carry no age-adjusted rate, so only unadjusted is comparable.

title: Veteran Suicide Rate By State
idea: Map of veteran suicide rate per 100k by state for the latest year, with the national rate as reference.
harm_angle: Where a veteran lives changes their odds of dying by suicide.
caveat: Suppressed small-count cells are null and will read as gaps, not zeros.

title: Veteran Excess Over Neighbors
idea: Map shaded by the difference between the veteran rate and the general-population rate in the same state.
harm_angle: Isolates the veteran-specific harm from a state overall suicide climate.
caveat: The two rate bases may not be age-standardized the same way.

title: States Getting Worse Fastest
idea: Slope chart of each state veteran rate at the first and last available year, ranked by deterioration.
harm_angle: States trending the wrong way over two decades show where services never arrived.
caveat: Small-state rates swing wildly on a handful of deaths.

title: Rural Region Burden
idea: Ranked bars by geographic region of veteran deaths per veteran population, testing the rural-access hypothesis.
harm_angle: Distance to a VA facility becomes a body count in low-density regions.
caveat: geographic_region grouping definition is unverified and rurality is inferred, not published.

title: Who Is In the New Payment Model
idea: Map participant counts by state and organization, split by asm_cohort and small-practice flag. Viewer sees which states have almost no participating specialists.
harm_angle: Patients in states with no participating specialists are excluded from whatever the model improves.
caveat: Forward-looking participation flags for future calendar years - not observed behavior.

title: Small Practices Dropping Out Year by Year
idea: Cohort grid of the CY27 through CY31 participant and small-practice flags per NPI. Viewer sees whether small practices are designated out over the model life.
harm_angle: If small practices exit, rural and low-income patients lose their only local specialist.
caveat: Future-year columns may be entirely blank at ingest time; flags are designations not outcomes.

title: Organizations Concentrating Participants
idea: Ranked bars of participating NPIs per organization_legal_name. Viewer sees the consolidated groups that dominate the model.
harm_angle: Payment models designed for practices end up run by a few large groups.
caveat: 6,637 rows; organization names need normalization.

source_names: CMS FISS Attending and Rendering Providers
title: Provider Roster Coverage Check
idea: Count distinct NPIs in the FISS roster and compare against the broader provider universe. Viewer sees how much of the billing provider population this roster actually holds.
harm_angle: A provider identity roster is the spine every Medicare-harm analysis depends on - its holes are the limits of what can be proven.
caveat: Genuinely thin: only three columns - NPI plus first and last name, no dates, no geography, no specialty. Nothing here has a human on the other end by itself.

source_names: CMS FISS Attending and Rendering Providers
title: Duplicate Names Across NPIs
idea: Find name pairs sharing a first and last name across multiple NPIs. Viewer sees the ambiguity that breaks name-based provider matching everywhere else.
harm_angle: Name collisions are how a sanctioned provider keeps billing under a clean identity.
caveat: Duplicate names are usually genuinely different people - a data-quality exhibit, not an accusation.

title: Where the historical maps look
idea: Map of the geographic coverage of the digitised historical maps to show which parts of the world the collection documents and which it ignores.
harm_angle: Whose places got mapped and archived determines whose history can be researched at all.
caveat: Only 10 rows in the mart — this is almost certainly a probe load not the real collection.

title: Publication era timeline
idea: Timeline of map publication dates showing the eras the collection concentrates on.
harm_angle: Gaps in the archived record are gaps in what can be proved about a place's past.
caveat: Ten rows makes any distribution meaningless; date_published likely free text.

title: Incarceration camps and their records
idea: Map of WWII Japanese American incarceration facilities sized by how many archived objects document each to show which camps are well documented and which nearly forgotten.
harm_angle: Camps with thin documentation are the ones whose survivors' experience is hardest to prove and easiest to deny.
caveat: Only 25 rows in the mart which suggests a sample rather than the full repository.

title: Object type mix over time
idea: Timeline or stacked bars of archived object type (photograph document oral history) by date to show what kind of evidence survives from which period.
harm_angle: Where only official documents survive and no personal testimony does the government's account is the only account.
caveat: 25 rows; date may be free text.

title: Topic coverage of the archive
idea: Ranked bars of topics by object count to show which parts of the incarceration story the archive covers deeply and which are thin.
harm_angle: Under-documented aspects of a mass incarceration are the aspects that vanish from public memory first.
caveat: Very small row count; topic may be a multi-value field.

title: Publication timeline of the corpus
idea: Timeline of publication dates across the corpus split by collection (slave narratives Southern literature church records) to show when each kind of source was produced.
harm_angle: When first-person narratives were published tells you when formerly enslaved people were allowed to be heard.
caveat: 144 rows; publication_date is likely free text with circa notations.

title: Authors and how many works survive
idea: Ranked bars of authors by number of works in the corpus to show whose voice the archive preserves most.
harm_angle: An archive dominated by a handful of authors misrepresents how many people were writing.
caveat: Author names are inconsistent and some works are anonymous.

title: Collection balance
idea: Distribution of works across collections to show whether the digitised Southern record is mostly white-authored literature or first-person narrative.
harm_angle: If the digitised Southern archive is mostly planter-class writing then the accessible history is the enslavers' version.
caveat: Only 144 rows in the mart which may be a fraction of the real corpus.

title: What NARA actually put online
idea: Ranked bars of NARA datasets by record count and series title to show how tiny the online-searchable slice of the federal record is.
harm_angle: Records the public cannot search are records the public cannot use to hold anyone accountable.
caveat: Only 18 rows so this is a catalog-of-datasets view not a records view.

title: Date span of the searchable record
idea: Timeline of record dates across the datasets to show which decades of the federal record are online.
harm_angle: Decades missing from the searchable record are decades of government action nobody can audit.
caveat: record_date derives from a text field and may be unparseable; tiny row count.

source_names: NARA WRA Records — Japanese American Relocation
title: Camp populations by origin
idea: Flow diagram from home county of origin to relocation camp showing which communities were emptied into which camps.
harm_angle: Mapping who was taken from where makes the scale and the targeting of a mass incarceration concrete.
caveat: Only 38 rows in this mart — the real WRA series is over a hundred thousand people so this is a probe load.

source_names: NARA WRA Records — Japanese American Relocation
title: Age and sex of the incarcerated
idea: Distribution of age by sex among incarcerated individuals to show how much of the camp population was children and elderly.
harm_angle: Showing the age pyramid makes plain that most people imprisoned as security risks were children and old people.
caveat: 38 rows; age may be text.

source_names: NARA WRA Records — Japanese American Relocation
title: Citizens versus non-citizens interned
idea: Ranked bars of camp by the share of internees who were US citizens to show that the majority imprisoned held American citizenship.
harm_angle: Most people incarcerated were US citizens which makes the camps a constitutional failure not an immigration measure.
caveat: Tiny extract; citizenship_status coding unverified.

source_names: NARA WRA Records — Japanese American Relocation
title: Families split across camps
idea: Network of family numbers linked to camps to reveal families separated into different facilities.
harm_angle: Family separation at scale was a deliberate feature of the camp system and the family numbers prove it.
caveat: 38 rows cannot support this; would need the full NARA series relanded.

title: Mortality rate by route
idea: Scatter of captives embarked against the voyage mortality rate coloured by embarkation region to show which intra-American routes killed the highest share.
harm_angle: Route-level mortality rates put a number on how many people specific merchants killed in transit.
caveat: Many voyage variables are sparsely populated across 11.5k voyages; imputed (IMP) columns mix estimate with record.

title: Ports that fed the internal trade
idea: Flow diagram from major buying port to major selling port sized by captives showing the internal American trafficking network.
harm_angle: The intra-American trade is the least-known leg and it moved people between colonies long after the Atlantic trade was banned.
caveat: Port codes need a lookup to readable names; the codebook is not in this table.

title: Trade volume after abolition
idea: Timeline of voyages and captives carried by year showing how the internal trade continued and grew after the transatlantic ban.
harm_angle: The trade did not stop when it was banned; it moved and the people moved with it.
caveat: YEARAM may be missing for many voyages; national flag coding needs a lookup.

title: Named captains and repeat voyages
idea: Ranked bars of captains by number of documented voyages and total captives carried to name the individuals who did this repeatedly.
harm_angle: Naming the repeat operators moves the record from an abstract system to individual accountable people.
caveat: Captain names are inconsistently spelled across records; entity resolution required.

title: Voyage fate and what happened to people aboard
idea: Distribution of voyage outcomes (delivered captured wrecked) against captives embarked to show how many people died in events that were never the voyage's purpose.
harm_angle: Shipwrecks and captures killed people whose deaths are recorded only as a change in cargo count.
caveat: Fate is a coded value needing a lookup; multiple fate columns overlap.

title: The full trade over three centuries
idea: Timeline of captives embarked and disembarked by year showing the volume of the transatlantic trade and the gap between the two lines that is the death toll.
harm_angle: The distance between embarked and disembarked is roughly two million people who died at sea.
caveat: Imputed columns mix documented values with statistical estimates; the distinction matters and is not obvious.

title: Flag nation by era
idea: Stacked timeline of voyages by carrier nation showing Portugal Britain France and the US trading places as the dominant trafficker.
harm_angle: Naming which nations carried the most people and when assigns responsibility to states that still exist.
caveat: National flag is coded and requires a lookup; flag of convenience distorts the attribution.

title: Children aboard
idea: Timeline or distribution of the child ratio aboard voyages over time showing the periods when traffickers filled ships with children.
harm_angle: The rising share of children aboard is a measurable choice by traffickers and children died at higher rates.
caveat: Ratio columns exist in several variants with different denominators; picking the wrong one distorts everything.

title: Mortality against voyage length
idea: Scatter of voyage duration against mortality rate coloured by route to show that longer crossings killed proportionally more people.
harm_angle: Every extra week at sea had a body count and shippers knew it and sailed anyway.
caveat: Date columns are numerous and inconsistently populated; duration must be derived and will be null for most voyages.

title: Crew deaths versus captive deaths
idea: Scatter of crew died against captive mortality per voyage to show the conditions were lethal to everyone aboard but catastrophically so for the imprisoned.
harm_angle: Comparing the two death rates on the same ship removes any argument that the deaths were unavoidable conditions.
caveat: CREWDIED is sparsely recorded; surviving records skew toward better-documented voyages.

title: Ports of arrival mapped
idea: Map of American arrival ports sized by total captives disembarked showing where the enslaved population of the Americas actually landed.
harm_angle: Naming the arrival ports connects present-day cities to the specific number of people landed there in chains.
caveat: Port codes need a geographic lookup not present in this table.

source_names: Born in Slavery: WPA Slave Narratives
title: Where the Interviewers Went
idea: Map the 1936-38 interview count by state and compare it against where enslaved people actually lived, showing which states the federal record barely touched.
harm_angle: Whole populations of formerly enslaved people are missing from the only federal record of their testimony.
caveat: Only 100 rows in the mart; may be a sample rather than the full ~2,300-narrative corpus.

source_names: Born in Slavery: WPA Slave Narratives
title: Who Held the Pen
idea: Ranked bars of interviewers by number of narratives collected, with each bar split by state, exposing how a handful of white federal writers shaped most of the archive.
harm_angle: The testimony of formerly enslaved people was filtered through a small set of government interviewers who chose what got written down.
caveat: interviewer may be sparsely populated or inconsistently formatted; 100-row mart limits ranking depth.

source_names: Born in Slavery: WPA Slave Narratives
title: How Long They Let Them Talk
idea: Distribution of narrative text length by state and interviewer, revealing whose accounts were transcribed at length and whose were cut to a paragraph.
harm_angle: Shorter transcripts mean a person's account of enslavement was truncated by the recorder, not by the speaker.
caveat: full_text may be null or truncated in the mart; char length is a proxy for effort, not a measure of it.

source_names: Born in Slavery: WPA Slave Narratives
title: The Interview Calendar
idea: Timeline of interviews by month across 1936-38, small-multipled by state, showing the bursts and long silences of the federal collection effort.
harm_angle: Gaps in the calendar are people who died before anyone came to ask.
caveat: interview_date may be partially null or text-derived; monthly grain may be too fine for 100 rows.

source_names: Born in Slavery: WPA Slave Narratives
title: Subject Tags as a Silence Map
idea: Heatmap grid of subject tags against state, showing which themes -- violence, family separation, wages -- were recorded where and which were systematically absent.
harm_angle: Themes missing from the tagging are the parts of enslavement the federal archive did not want indexed.
caveat: subjects is likely a free-text or array field needing parsing; tagging may be a modern librarian layer, not a 1930s choice.

source_names: HMDA Home Mortgage Disclosure Act Data
title: Denial Rate by Race in One City
idea: Ranked bars of mortgage denial rate by derived race and ethnicity within a single metro, holding loan purpose constant, so the gap is visible at equal product.
harm_angle: Applicants of color denied at higher rates for the same product are being priced out of homeownership by the lender, not the market.
caveat: Mart is a DC-2023 sample only -- the model file explicitly says never use for lending-pattern claims until a full state-by-year pull lands.

source_names: HMDA Home Mortgage Disclosure Act Data
title: Rate Spread vs Income by Race
idea: Scatter of rate spread against applicant income, colored by derived race, to show whether Black and Hispanic borrowers pay more at the same income level.
harm_angle: Higher rate spreads at identical income means the borrower pays thousands more over the life of the loan for their race.
caveat: rate_spread and income are kept as text in staging; DC-only sample kills any national claim; income is applicant-reported.

source_names: HMDA Home Mortgage Disclosure Act Data
title: Why They Said No
idea: Flow diagram from applicant demographic group to the stated denial reason, showing whether 'credit history' vs 'debt-to-income' reasons are applied unevenly.
harm_angle: If the same denial reason is disproportionately assigned to one group, the reason code itself is doing discriminatory work.
caveat: denial_reason fields are coded numerics needing a codebook; only populated for denied applications; DC-only slice.

source_names: HMDA Home Mortgage Disclosure Act Data
title: Lender Fingerprints on One Map
idea: Small multiples of census tracts, one panel per lender, shading each tract by that lender's approval rate -- lenders with holes in the same neighborhoods stand out.
harm_angle: Neighborhoods that every lender skips are being redlined in effect even where no lender did it alone.
caveat: LEI populated-ness unverified; DC-only sample means few lenders and thin tract counts.

source_names: HMDA Home Mortgage Disclosure Act Data
title: Costs Rise as Tract Whiteness Falls
idea: Scatter of total loan costs and discount points against tract minority population percent, with a fitted trend, to test whether closing costs climb in non-white tracts.
harm_angle: Extra thousands in fees charged in non-white neighborhoods is a direct transfer of wealth out of those households.
caveat: Cost fields are text in staging and often blank for exempt lenders; DC-only slice; costs scale with loan size and need normalizing.

title: Denied After The Flood
idea: County map of the share of disaster-aid registrations found ineligible for housing assistance revealing where aid systematically does not land.
harm_angle: Households whose homes flooded and who got nothing are the clearest case of harm the data can show.
caveat: Mart is a 12 percent truncated load, not a random sample, so geography may be skewed.

title: Aid Award Versus Verified Loss
idea: Scatter of verified real property loss against the actual award amount with the assistance cap drawn as a ceiling line showing households hitting the cap far below their loss.
harm_angle: Every point below the diagonal is a family told their loss exceeds what the government will pay.
caveat: Truncated 12 percent load; verified-loss fields may be zero for uninspected registrations.

title: Renters Get Less Than Owners
idea: Small multiples by disaster comparing award distributions for owners versus renters at similar damage levels.
harm_angle: Renters displaced by the same storm may be structurally awarded less than their homeowner neighbors.
caveat: Damage-level scales differ between owner and renter records, so the comparison needs care.

title: Unmet Need Left On The Table
idea: Ranked bars of disasters by total unmet need for personal and real property next to total assistance actually paid.
harm_angle: Unmet need is the government's own count of harm it chose not to cover.
caveat: Truncated load means disaster totals are understated and not comparable across disasters.

title: Income And The Inspection Outcome
